A smaller, third ulcer was also noted in the intergluteal cleft. B, Microscopic examination of the punch biopsy on low magnification reveals epidermal ulceration and mixed dermal inflammation (hemoxylin-eosin. C, On higher magnification, the epidermis lacks viral cytopathic changes but there are enlarged dermal fibroblasts and endothelial cells (hemoxylin-eosin). D, Higher magnification reveals large fibroblasts and endothelial cells with glassy cytoplasm and intranuclear inclusions (hemoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A woman in her late 30s was evaluated by the dermatology inpatient consult service for a 4-day history of perianal pain. Her medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, and external hemorrhoids. Six months before admission, she underwent a deceased donor kidney transplant. One month before presentation, she was hospitalized for acute cellular transplant rejection managed with systemic corticosteroids, belatacept, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus therapies. Her immunosuppressive regimen at the time of dermatologic evaluation consisted of prednisone, 5 mg daily, and mycophenolate mofetil, 500 mg twice daily. On admission, she was afebrile and normotensive; laboratory results were notable for an elevated creatinine level of 1.43 mg/dL (reference range, 0.40-1.30 mg/dL) (to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count, 92 × 103/μL [reference range, 140-440 × 103/μL] [conversion to ×109per liter is 1:1). She developed diarrhea 1 day after admission. Fecal leukocytes were absent. Stool antigen test results for cryptosporidium, giardia, and rotavirus were negative. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test results for campylobacter, norovirus, salmonella, shigella, Shiga toxin–producingEscherichia coli1 and 2,Vibrio cholerae, andYersinia enterocoliticain the stool were negative. Antigen and toxin test results forClostridium difficilein the stool were positive. Total body skin examination was notable for 1- and 3-cm tender, round perianal ulcers with a clean base. Another 4-mm round ulcer was present at the superior intergluteal cleft (Figure, A). There were no ocular or oral ulcers. A biopsy specimen of a perianal ulcer border was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B-D).
explanation: Examination of a punch biopsy specimen revealed epidermal ulceration with mixed dermal inflammation (Figure, B and C). There were large fibroblasts and endothelial cells with glassy cytoplasm and large intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo, giving the “owl’s eye” appearance (Figure, D). Inclusions were positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) immunohistochemical stain. Quantitative PCR results demonstrated a CMV load of 172 000 copies/mL (5.24 log10IU/mL) in the blood. A PCR swab from the ulcer base was positive for CMV. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of cutaneous ulceration secondary to CMV infection was made. A common infectious complication after renal transplant, CMV increases the risk for allograft rejection.1As with this patient, CMV-seronegative patients who receive renal transplants from seropositive donors are at highest risk of hospitalization from CMV disease.1In patients who receive a transplant, CMV infection may lead to significant morbidity and mortality, most notably owing to CMV colitis. This patient had diarrhea; however, the diagnosis of CMV colitis was obscured by concurrentC difficilecolitis. While CMV infection rarely presents in the skin, in immunosuppressed patients protean skin manifestations, including cutaneous vasculitis, morbilliform eruption, ulcers, petechiae, purpura, vesicles, and plaques, may be the presenting sign of disseminated disease.2The anogenital region is the most common site of cutaneous ulceration, likely because of fecal shedding of viral particles.2On histopathology, CMV initially shows an enlarged nucleus, then an enlarged cytoplasm, followed by intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions. In resolving lesions, cells diminish in size and inclusions fade away.3 The diagnostic criterion standard for CMV is identification of inclusions or viral antigens on histopathologic examination. When examination of a biopsy specimen is inconclusive, tissue culture and viral load may aid in diagnosis.4In a recent series, CMV was detected via PCR swab in 4 of 4 patients who developed cutaneous lesions.5Herpes simplex virus (HSV) can cause perianal ulcers, and coinfection may be seen with CMV.2However, the biopsy specimen from this patient did not reveal ballooning degeneration or multinucleation of keratinocytes with the typical cytopathic intranuclear Cowdry type A (eosinophilic) or Cowdry type B (“steel gray”) inclusions of HSV. Moreover, immunohistochemical stain and PCR test results were negative for HSV. Amebiasis cutis, an extension of colonicEntamoeba histolyticainfection, may present with painful, serpiginous perianal ulcers with raised borders.6Histopathologic examination reveals amebic trophozoites with a small nucleus and erythrophagocytosis, findings that were absent in this case. Finally, cutaneous Crohn disease could be considered; however, the ulcers were not “knifelike” and noncaseating granulomas were not observed on histopathologic examination. A graft transplant from a seronegative donor to a seronegative recipient is ideal to prevent CMV disease. When not feasible, a preventive approach involving prophylactic doses of oral ganciclovir, valganciclovir, letermovir, valacyclovir, or CMV immune globulin therapies can be used.7Alternatively, preemptive treatment with intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir therapy is administered after detection of CMV infection on weekly testing. Intravenous ganciclovir therapy is first-line treatment for CMV disease; however, CMV cutaneous ulcers have been successfully treated with oral valganciclovir therapy.8Cidofovir or foscarnet therapy can be useful in patients with ganciclovir-resistant CMV infection. The CMV vaccine candidates in development have recently shown promise in transplanted patients, decreasing the durations of viremia and ganciclovir treatment.9 This patient had a history of ganciclovir-resistant CMV after renal transplant; therefore, foscarnet, 40 mg/kg, IV therapy was initiated along with oral vancomycin forC difficilecolitis. The patient’s diarrhea resolved within 24 hours. Subsequent quantitative PCR after 4 days of foscarnet therapy demonstrated a CMV viral load of 13 300 copies/mL (4.13 log10IU/mL) in the blood. She reported improvement in perianal pain and the ulcers decreased in size. She continued with foscarnet therapy until discharge 3 weeks later, and her medication was transitioned to oral letermovir therapy, 480 mg daily. She remained asymptomatic 3 months after discharge.

caption: A, Large, well-defined, firm yellow to skin-colored multinodular hypertrichotic plaque on the left lower back. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrates diffuse dermal infiltration of spindle cells, predominantly encircling terminal folliculosebaceous units (original magnification ×4). C, Higher-power magnification highlights a mix of partially fusiform melanocytes and dendritic cells with glassy, eosinophilic cytoplasm (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×40). D, Immunohistochemical staining reveals diffuse and periadnexal S100 positivity in the mid to deep dermis (original magnification ×4).
scenario: A 17-month-old boy was referred to pediatric dermatology for evaluation of a slow-growing, nontender plaque on the lower back. The child's mother reported that, on discovery, the plaque was initially 1 × 1 cm and had since grown in size with the child. She was uncertain if the plaque was present at birth. The patient’s medical history was significant for dermal melanocytosis of the right hip and mid back, increased head circumference (97th percentile), and expressive language delay. There was no family history of congenital birthmarks or neurofibromatosis type 1 or 2. Physical examination revealed a well-appearing boy with normal vital signs and Fitzpatrick type III skin type. On the left lower back, there was a 15 × 5-cm indurated skin-colored to yellow, firm, multinodular plaque with hypertrichosis, extending from the midline to the left lower flank (Figure, A). There were additional blue-gray patches on the back and right hip, as well as a small café au lait macule on the right lower back. Limited neurologic examination was within normal limits. A 4-mm punch biopsy was performed for further diagnostic evaluation (Figure, B-D).
explanation: Histopathologic evaluation findings demonstrated a diffuse dermal proliferation of partially fusiform spindled cells in the mid to deep dermis with entrapped enlarged terminal folliculosebaceous units. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for S100, CD34, and SOX-10 and negative for desmin, SMA, and CD1a. Partial expression of Melan A and epithelial membrane antigen stains were noted. This combination of clinical and histopathologic examination findings led to a diagnosis of neurocristic hamartoma. A magnetic resonance image of the lumbar spine was obtained, which showed a contrast-enhancing cutaneous lesion extending between the L3 and L5 spinal segment, with branches of enhancement extending into the paraspinous soft tissues of the L4 and the deep subcutaneous tissues of the L3 spinous process. There was no evidence of spinal involvement or dysraphism. Because the lesion extended into the deep subcutaneous tissue of the L3 to L5 spinal segments, annual magnetic resonance imaging surveillance was recommended, with a low threshold for rebiopsy if pigment or new features emerged. Neurocristic hamartomas (NCHs) are rare collections of dermal neuromesenchymal cells of neural crest origin. While NCHs were initially thought to be variants of blue nevi, they are now known to have unique clinical and histologic features.1Neurocristic hamartoma is derived from the aberrant differentiation of pluriopotent neural crest cells into Schwann cells, melanocytes, and pigmented dendritic cells.2While typically congenital, NCH may be acquired from sites of constant pluripotent-cell activation.2 Neurocristic hamartomas present similarly to blue nevi, typically as blue-to-black hyperpigmented plaques on the head or neck with focal alopecia.3While the majority of cases are seen on the scalp, NCHs have been reported to occur on the back and face.4Neurocristic hamartomas may overlap with other disorders of neural crest, including neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and neurocutaneous melanosis.2Of 32 cases of NCH reported in the literature, 12 (38%) had malignant transformation into melanoma and 6 (19%) metastasized.4-6Genetic analysis of malignant NCH has demonstrated a lack ofBRAF,GNAQ,NRAS, andKITmutations, suggesting a separate mechanism for malignant transformation compared with malignant melanoma.6Histologically, NCHs have overlapping features with blue nevi, including heavily pigmented spindled cells with a fusiform appearance and a predilection for adnexal structures.1However, NCHs have additional neural and Schwann cell differentiation.1Neurocristic hamartomas stain positive for S100, HMB-45, and CD-34 markers in the stroma.2,4 Becker nevus (BN) is a solitary hyperpigmented plaque with male predilection that may involve any region of the body. Becker nevus arises during the first decade of life, often developing hypertrichosis during the second decade of life because of its androgen-dependent nature. Becker nevus may be associated with hypoplasia or hyperplasia, or asymmetry of the affected area.7In this patient, while both BN and the NCH appeared in the first decade with hypertrichosis, BN exhibits epidermal hypermelanosis and acanthosis with few melanocytes in the dermis. Smooth muscle hamartoma (SMH) is a congenital, solitary hyperpigmented and hypertrichotic plaque commonly involving the trunk, buttocks, and lower extremities. These are distinguished from similar lesions by a positive pseudo-Darier sign. Malignant transformation has not been reported.8While both NCH and SMH can present as solitary hyperpigmented and hypertrichotic plaques, SMHs display as collections of spindled smooth muscle cells throughout the dermis, in contrast to the collection of neural crest–derived cells in NCH. Plexiform neurofibromas (PNs) are associated with NF1 and present as tender, firm subcutaneous nodules with a “bag of worms” consistency that span along the length of peripheral nerves. Superficial PNs may be characterized by hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis, easily confused for congenital melanocytic nevi. Approximately 8% to 12% of patients with NF1 develop malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors from PNs, with the potential to infiltrate into nerves, muscle, and fascia.9Although both PNs and NCHs can demonstrate S100 positivity, the patient described herein had a diffuse proliferation of spindled cells in contrast to the clear fascicles present in PN. Neurocristic hamartoma is a rare diagnosis that should be considered on the differential for hypertrichotic plaques in children as well in cases of focal alopecia, such as aplasia cutis, especially because that is a more common clinical presentation. Owing to the paucity of reported cases, long-term management is not well understood. However, given the possibility of malignant transformation, periodic skin examinations are recommended.

caption: Multiple skin-colored and erythematous follicular papules are seen coalescing into a linear plaque involving the patient’s forehead, as well as the dorsum and tip of the nose (A). Two skin punch biopsies were taken from the forehead and nose (B and C).
scenario: A girl younger than 2 years presented with a 1-year history of slightly pruritic lesions involving her face. She was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, and her growth and development were appropriate for her age. No associated symptoms such as fever, anorexia, or weight loss were noted. Physical examination revealed multiple skin-colored and erythematous follicular papules, 1 to 2 mm in diameter, distributed in a segmental pattern on the right side of the forehead, as well as the dorsum and tip of the nose. A small, excoriated plaque was also noted on the right malar area (Figure 1A). No mucosal lesions were present, and the rest of the physical examination findings were unremarkable. A complete hematological and biochemical survey, including blood cell count, liver and renal function tests, C-reactive protein levels, thyroid function, rheumatoid factor, and antinuclear antibodies, disclosed no abnormalities. Two skin punch biopsies were taken from the forehead and nose. Representative histopathological features are shown inFigure 1B and C.
explanation: Histopathological examination revealed accumulation of a finely granular basophilic material within the follicular and sebaceous gland epithelium. A moderate perivascular and periadnexal infiltrate of lymphocytes, lacking cytological atypia, was observed in the superficial and mid dermis. There was no epidermotropism nor vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer. Results of Alcian blue stain demonstrated the presence of mucin. Clinicopathological correlation supported the diagnosis of idiopathic follicular mucinosis (IFM). The patient was treated with topical corticosteroid and tacrolimus, 0.03%, without improvement. Systemic corticosteroids at a daily dosage of 0.5 mg/kg were then initiated with complete resolution of the lesions but recurrence after withdrawal. The patients’ parents declined more intensive therapy, and the lesions resolved spontaneously. Eighteen months after diagnosis, the patient remained in clinical remission (Figure 2). Idiopathic follicular mucinosis is an uncommon condition characterized by lymphocytic folliculotropism associated with the deposition of mucin within the pilosebaceous unit. The disease predominantly affects adults and is clinically manifested by follicular papules and plaques, usually involving the head and neck, and sometimes associating nonscarring alopecia.1-3 Histologically, IFM is characterized by mucin deposition within the follicular and sebaceous gland epithelium, along with a periadnexal infiltrate of lymphocytes. Epidermotropism and folliculotropism can be prominent, but a bandlike lymphocytic infiltrate along the papillary dermis, Pautrier microabscesses, and marked lymphocyte atypia are usually absent.1,4,5Immunohistological findings reveal a predominance of helper T cells (CD3+, CD4+, and CD8−), and up to 50% of cases show a monoclonal pattern of T-cell receptor gene rearrangement.1,2 The differential diagnosis includes lymphoma-associated follicular mucinosis, especially with folliculotropic mycosis fungoides. Distinction between these 2 entities is extremely difficult because there are no reliable clinical, histological, or molecular findings alone to accurately allow a correct diagnosis.1,5In fact, IFM is sometimes considered to be a manifestation of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. In general, younger age; isolated lesions, especially on the head and neck; rapid response and resolution after systemic therapy; and absence of epidermotropism and lymphoid atypia suggest the diagnosis of IFM, while multiple lesions and those located in the extremities should raise the suspicion of lymphoma. Unfortunately, immunohistopathologic studies and T-cell receptor gene rearrangements do not help in the diagnosis.1,2,5Most lymphoma experts view the patient's age as the most important consideration in diagnosing IFM because children and adults younger than 40 years usually show a benign course without any evidence of progression. Furthermore, diagnosis of lymphoma-associated follicular mucinosis in children should be made with caution because there are cases of IFM fulfilling diagnostic criteria for mycosis fungoides but showing spontaneous resolution and excellent prognosis.5 The present case is unusual as, to the best of our knowledge, IFM presenting in a segmental or blaschkoid distribution has not been previously described. Lymphoproliferative disorders showing this peculiar presentation are rare and represent a diagnostic challenge because it can be misdiagnosed as several inflammatory skin conditions.6-8Other differential diagnosis include lichen striatus, follicular mucinous nevus, and trichodysplasia spinulosa. Lichen striatus is characterized by epidermal spongiosis and vacuolar degeneration of the dermoepidermal junction. Follicular mucinous nevus is a rare type of follicular hamartoma that also shows mucin deposition; however, in follicular mucinous nevus, the mucin deposition is restricted to the follicular epithelium and does not involve the glandular adnexal epithelia. Additionally, there is a fibromucinous stroma in the papillary and perifollicular dermis.9Finally, trichodysplasia spinulosa almost exclusively affects immunocompromised individuals and histologically shows large eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions within the cells of the inner root sheath. Several treatment modalities, with variable results, have been described for IFM, including corticosteroids, dapsone, hydroxychloroquine, and interferon alpha.10Because IFD is a benign condition, no aggressive treatment is recommended. However, given the difficulty in distinguishing it from lymphoma, long-term follow-up is warranted.

caption: A, Infiltrative plaques and nodules obscuring normal facial architecture. B and C, Histopathologic images show normal epidermis with dense diffuse dermal lymphoid infiltrate composed of small to medium cells with irregular nuclear contours (hematoxylin-eosin stain). scenario: A man in his 60s presented as a transfer from an outside hospital. The division of dermatology was consulted for evaluation of lesions on the face, chest, back, and arms that were gradually increasing in size and number over the past year. Physical examination revealed leonine facies with madarosis and an eschar on the nasal dorsum (Figure, A). Red-to-brown dome-shaped papules coalescing into plaques were present on the upper extremities. The lesions were nontender and nonpruritic. Cervical and axillary lymph nodes were palpable. The patient had a muffled voice and reported shortness of breath with exertion. Results of laboratory investigation demonstrated marked leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 77.5 × 103/uL with 76.5% lymphocytes. No blasts were present on peripheral smear. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated multiple enlarged mediastinal, axillary, subpectoral, abdominopelvic, and inguinal lymph nodes. Small pulmonary nodules were also detected. A punch biopsy was obtained from the right arm (Figure, B, C, and D).
explanation: Histopathological findings revealed normal epidermis with a dense diffuse dermal infiltrate of small to medium lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours. Results of CD20 and cyclin D1 stains were diffusely positive. The patient had been diagnosed with stage IV mantle cell lymphoma 2 years prior to presentation on the basis of a lymph node biopsy in the setting of unexplained weight loss and night sweats. Further investigation including fluorescence in situ hybridization testing and flow cytometry was confirmatory. The patient was previously treated at an outside institution, and multiple courses of chemotherapy had failed. On admission, the patient was started on treatment with high-dose steroids intravenously. Despite this, he developed upper airway obstruction and was intubated. He then became febrile, encephalopathic, and nonresponsive. He subsequently died in hospice. Mantle cell lymphoma is a rare type of non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma. It is characterized by a cytogenetic translocation resulting in overexpression of the cyclin D1 protein, which is required for progression from G1 to S phase of the cell cycle.1Mantle cell lymphoma often involves extranodal sites, including the bone marrow, gastrointestinal tract, and Waldeyer ring. In this patient, involvement of the Waldeyer ring led to upper airway obstruction that necessitated intubation. Men older than 60 years are the most commonly affected demographic. Mantle cell lymphoma is often aggressive and portends a poor prognosis. The median survival time after diagnosis is 4 to 5 years.1 Histologic features include diffuse monomorphous infiltrates of intermediate-sized lymphocytes with irregular nuclei and nucleoli. The immunophenotype of malignant B-cells involves coexpression of CD20, CD5, and cyclin D1, which is positive in more than 95% of cases. In rare cyclin D1–negative cases, SOX11 can be a useful diagnostic marker.2,3In addition, CD23 expression is often absent and is useful in distinguishing mantle cell lymphoma from chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Cutaneous involvement by mantle cell lymphoma is rare and occurs as secondary dissemination in stage IV disease. Approximately 17% of stage IV cases will exhibit skin involvement.4Typically, cutaneous mantle cell lymphoma presents with solitary or multiple nodules. Leonine facies is an exceedingly rare presentation, with only 1 prior case reported to our knowledge.5The differential diagnosis for leonine facies is broad and includes entities such as lepromatous leprosy, scleromyxedema, lipoid proteinosis, nonlangerhans cell histiocytosis, and pachydermoperiostosis, in addition to cutaneous lymphoma. Subtypes of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma have been reported to present in this manner, including folliculotropic mycosis fungoides, classic mycosis fungoides, and Sézary syndrome. Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides can be distinguished histopathologically by the presence of atypical lymphocytes invading the follicular epithelium. In addition, immunohistochemistry demonstrates CD3 and CD4 positivity with loss of CD7.6 Less commonly, B-cell lymphomas may present with leonine facies. In such cases, histopathology and immunohistochemistry can be used to differentiate between subtypes. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma often displays a dense dermal infiltrate of large, atypical lymphocytes that variably express BCL2, MUM1, FOXP1, and MYC. Marginal zone lymphoma is typically characterized by nodular dermal infiltrates surrounded by pale small to medium lymphocytes with indented nuclei. Cells typically stain positively for BCL2 and negatively for BCL6 and CD10. Cases of mantle cell lymphoma are uniquely distinguished by expression of cyclin D1, a highly sensitive and specific marker. In summary, skin involvement by mantle cell lymphoma is rare yet important to recognize because it signifies disseminated disease and an aggressive clinical course. It is crucial to differentiate this entity from primary cutaneous B-cell lymphomas, such as marginal zone lymphoma and follicle center lymphoma, which may be localized to the skin and often exhibit indolent behavior. Careful analysis of histopathologic features, immunohistochemical studies, and correlation with systemic diagnostic examination are necessary to establish the diagnosis.

scenario: A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

scenario: A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

scenario: A 2-month-old boy, born at 39 weeks 1 day of gestation via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery with normal newborn screening results presented with a 10-day history of rash. On presentation, his temperature was 37.0 °C (98.6 °F); blood pressure, 113/74 mm Hg; and heart rate, 132 beats/min. Skin examination showed multiple annular, pink papules and plaques with hyperpigmentation and desquamation on the scalp, palms, and soles (Figure 1). Physical examination showed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing revealed elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (238 U/L [reference, 9-80 U/L]) (3.97 μkat/L [reference, 0.15-1.34 μkat/L]) and alanine aminotransferase (261 U/L [reference, 13-45 U/L]) (4.36 μkat/L [reference, 0.22-0.75 μkat/L). Results of testing for antinuclear antibody, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Of note, his mother had a negative rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test at 12 and 32 weeks of pregnancy and a negative HIV test at 12 weeks of pregnancy.

explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

explanation: Coxiella burnetiiendocarditis (Q fever endocarditis) B. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Cardiac FDG PET/CT demonstrated circumferentially increased metabolic activity in the area of the prosthetic valve, suggestive of aortic root abscess (Figure 2). The patient developed intermittent grade 2 AV block. Three weeks after initial presentation, she underwent cardiac aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. No aortic root abscess was noted during surgery. Vegetations were detected on the explanted aortic valve, and polymerase chain reaction assay of the specimen was strongly positive forC burnetii(1 256 990 copies/mL). At 6-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic, C-reactive protein level was normal, andC burnetiiantibody titers had decreased to 1:5120 for phase I IgG and 1:640 for phase II IgG. Treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine is planned for a duration of 24 months.2

Intravenous heparin (choice A) is contraindicated because anticoagulation increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage in patients with moyamoya disease. Lumbar puncture (choice C) is not recommended because there are no clinical signs of infection. Choice D is not indicated because steroids are not effective treatment for moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA), leading to fragile collateral vessel formation.1﻿Moyamoya(Japanese for “puff of smoke”) refers to the angiographic findings of this abnormal vascular network.2 Moyamoya disease occurs in 0.1 per 100 000 people worldwide, but the prevalence is substantially higher in East Asia, especially Japan (17.6 per 100 000).3Moyamoya disease is approximately 2-fold more common among females than males and has a bimodal age distribution (at 10 years and 30 to 50 years).4A family history of moyamoya disease is reported in 12% to 15% of patients with the disease.3 Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are unknown but may involve alterations in genes involved in vascular development and angiogenesis, includingMMP,VEGF, andPDGFRB. TheRNF213p.R4810K gene variant increases the risk of moyamoya disease among East Asian patients.4 Patients with moyamoya disease may have intermittent transient ischemic attacks and strokes typically involving border zone areas or have hemorrhagic events (intracranial or intraventricular) due to rupture of fragile reticular vessels. Headaches affect 20% to 76.4% of patients, often with migraine-like features such as unilaterality and aura.5The differential diagnosis includes atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, autoimmune conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome), and infectious vasculopathies (eg, meningitis, cytomegalovirus infection). The diagnosis of moyamoya disease is made based on digital subtraction angiographic findings of (1) stenosis or occlusion of arteries in the terminal portion of the intracranial ICA and (2) abnormal vascular networks in the vicinity of the stenotic lesions. Brain MRI or MRA are less accurate for diagnosis, particularly in patients with unilateral lesions, those older than 60 years, or those with early-stage moyamoya disease.6 There is no curative treatment for moyamoya disease. Among patients presenting with ischemic events, surgical revascularization with a direct bypass (extracranial-intracranial anastomosis) or indirect bypass (eg, placement of superficial temporal artery onto the brain surface to promote new blood vessel growth) is associated with decreased risk of ischemic stroke and death. Patients receiving nonsurgical management of ischemic events have recurrent annual stroke rates of 20% to 50%.7 Asymptomatic patients with moyamoya disease have a 1.4% to 15% annual risk of stroke.7,8For these patients, bypass surgery is associated with a 26% reduction in the risk of death but a 76% increase in the risk of hemorrhagic events compared with nonsurgical management.7 Per 2021 Japanese guidelines, based on limited evidence (grade C), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, or cilostazol) can be considered to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with moyamoya disease and a history of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, those awaiting surgery, or those ineligible for surgery due to advanced age or comorbidities.9Endovascular treatment (angioplasty and/or stent) is associated with restenosis rates of 68.8%, and high rates (9.5%) of complications such as vessel rupture and intracerebral hemorrhage.10 Digital subtraction angiography revealed an abnormal net-like vascular network with a “smoke puff” appearance near the stenotic terminal portion of the ICA bilaterally (Figure 2and video). The patient received aspirin (75 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg). Seven days after initial presentation, she developed a new stroke and underwent an indirect bypass revascularization procedure. On postoperative day 21, she developed a right MCA ischemic stroke causing left hemiplegia. Two years later, she developed right-sided hemiparesis due to occlusion of the first segment of the left MCA and underwent direct bypass connecting the left superficial temporal artery to the left MCA. Four years after initial presentation, she has persistent left hemiparesis and a left steppage gait. Genetic testing revealed no pathogenic variants.

scenario: A 34-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, typically lasting 3 to 5 days and occurring approximately every 6 months. The pain was crampy and diffuse; accompanied by mild abdominal distension without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or hematochezia; and not relieved by eating or defecation. She reported no past medical history, allergies, or use of prescription or illicit drugs. On presentation, her temperature was 36.7 °C (98.06 °F); blood pressure, 120/78 mm Hg; and heart rate, 97 beats/min. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. She had mild, nonpitting painless swelling on the dorsum of both hands, accompanied by pruritus. Laboratory testing revealed normal hemoglobin level and normal liver and kidney function and urinalysis results. Serum complement C4 level was 5.31 mg/dL (reference, 14-36 mg/dL). Levels of antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and immunoglobulin were normal. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) performed during an episode of abdominal pain showed jejunal wall edema and ascites (Figure 1). Gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and small bowel endoscopy revealed no mucosal abnormalities. The patient reported that her father and brother experienced similar unexplained recurrent episodes of abdominal pain.

options.B: Check C1 inhibitor level and function
options.D: Perform deep endoscopic biopsy of the small bowel

answer: Check C1 inhibitor level and function
distractors: Administer methylprednisolone (60 mg intravenously daily for 3 days)
Perform deep endoscopic biopsy of the small bowel
explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

scenario: A 25-year-old woman with migraines for 10 years presented with palpitations, fatigue, and worsening migraines. Her heart rate was 93 beats/min and blood pressure was 120/92 mm Hg. Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram results were normal. Subsequent 48-hour Holter monitoring showed sinus tachycardia with a mean heart rate of 108 beats/min. Metoprolol succinate (25 mg daily) was started. Six months later, she was admitted to the hospital with 1 day of fevers, nausea, and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. Her temperature was 38.7 °C (101.7 °F); heart rate, 103 beats/min; and blood pressure, 138/89 mm Hg. Abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) showed a left anterior pararenal retroperitoneal mass. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with and without intravenous contrast showed a 4.0 × 3.5–cm T1 and T2 hypointense, enhancing infrarenal left para-aortic mass without local tissue or vascular invasion (Figure). Plasma normetanephrine concentration was 907 pg/mL (reference, 0-145 pg/mL) and plasma metanephrine concentration was within reference range.

options.D: Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control)

answer: Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control)
explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

scenario: A 34-year-old woman presented with 1 year of progressive skin tightening over her right elbow and forearm, bilateral forearm and anterior tibia pain, and difficulty extending her fingers and elbows. She had no history of autoimmune disease, diabetes, Raynaud phenomenon, or trauma, but her symptoms worsened after playing tennis. Six months prior, she received prednisone (40 mg daily for 3 days), which mildly improved her forearm and anterior tibia pain and decreased her skin tightening for several days. Physical examination revealed right forearm induration with linear depressions (Figure), hypopigmented plaque with violaceous borders over the right elbow, bilateral hand swelling, and skin tightening over the bilateral forearms and anterior tibia region. She had no digital pitting or skin tightening over her face or fingers. Laboratory testing revealed elevated eosinophil count (530 cells/μL) (reference, 100-500/μL), aldolase level (9.5 U/L [0.16 μkat/L]) (reference, 1.0-7.5 U/L [0.02-0.13 μkat/L]), and C-reactive protein level (9.3 mg/L) (reference, 0.0-5.0 mg/L), with normal results for complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, creatine kinase level, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:320 (reference, ≤1:80) with a speckled pattern, and results of an extractable nuclear antigen antibodies panel were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated increased signal of the superficial and deep myofascial planes in the extensor compartments of the forearm on fluid-sensitive, fat-saturated sequences.

options.A: Apply topical clobetasol to forearm twice daily for 7 days
options.B: Initiate 2 g/kg of intravenous immunoglobulin therapy
options.D: Treat with mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg twice daily)

distractors: Apply topical clobetasol to forearm twice daily for 7 days
Initiate 2 g/kg of intravenous immunoglobulin therapy
Treat with mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg twice daily)
explanation: C. Prescribe 40-mg prednisone daily for 14 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the presence of a linear depression along a superficial vein, visible when the forearm is raised, which is characteristic of eosinophilic fasciitis. Topical clobetasol (choice A) is incorrect because eosinophilic fasciitis consists of deeper fascial sclerosis that is not adequately treated by topical steroids.1,2High-dose immunoglobulin (choice B) and mycophenolate mofetil (choice D) are not first-line treatments for eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis is rare, with fewer than 600 reported cases worldwide, has no known etiology, and typically affects adults aged 30 to 60 years.4Patients initially develop subacute pain, erythema, and nonpitting edema of limbs or trunk that progresses to symmetric deep, woody skin induration over months to years.4Collagenous thickening of the subcutaneous fascia gives the skin an “orange peel” appearance.4Fibrosis and tethering of connective tissue around superficial veins cause the venous groove sign—a linear depression resulting from overlying epidermis being pulled inward along a vein.4 Eosinophilic fasciitis is associated with hematologic malignancies (eg, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma), graft-vs-host disease, hemodialysis initiation, radiation therapy, and  sustained intense physical exertion such as running. Based on case reports and small case series, certain medications are associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), statins, and proton pump inhibitors (eg, esomeprazole, lansoprazole).3,5 The criterion standard for the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis is presence of dermal and fascial fibrosis with or without eosinophils on a wedge biopsy that includes skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia.1However, in some cases the diagnosis may be made clinically in patients who have nonpitting edema or symmetric induration in distal limbs; MRI findings of fascial thickening with hyperintense T2 signal and contrast enhancement; and supportive but nonspecific laboratory findings, such as elevated inflammatory markers (eg, C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and hypergammaglobulinemia.4,6Prior to treatment with steroids, most patients initially have peripheral eosinophilia.3,7 The differential diagnosis includes systemic sclerosis, scleromyxedema and scleredema, and eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (associated with consumption of L-tryptophan or 5-hydroxytryptophan supplements).4,8Patients with eosinophilic fasciitis have cutaneous fibrosis but lack other characteristic features of systemic sclerosis, including digital and facial skin sclerosis, nailfold capillary abnormalities, Raynaud phenomenon, visceral involvement (eg, esophageal dysfunction, interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis), and specific autoantibodies such as antitopoisomerase I (Scl-70), anticentromere, anti-RNA polymerase III, and anti-U3-RNP (fibrillarin).4Differentiating eosinophilic fasciitis from systemic sclerosis is important because in patients with systemic sclerosis, steroids can trigger renal crisis, which involves a sudden-onset, severe increase in blood pressure and rapid decline in kidney function.9 First-line treatment for eosinophilic fasciitis is oral prednisone (0.5-1 mg/kg daily), although 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg) may be used in severe cases.7Steroid doses are tapered based on clinical response, and more than 70% of patients have complete resolution of cutaneous swelling after taking prednisone for several months, although the groove sign may persist several years after treatment.2,4Immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil may be added for extensive disease or to help taper or discontinue steroids.4,9,10Based on case series, tocilizumab, baricitinib, infliximab, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulins may be effective for severe eosinophilic fasciitis.3Physical therapy to prevent limb contractures is recommended for all patients with eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis was diagnosed based on the patient’s history, venous groove sign, and characteristic findings on MRI. After 1 month of treatment with oral prednisone (40 mg daily), she gained 4.54 kg (10 lb), so oral methotrexate (20 mg weekly) with folic acid (1 mg daily) was initiated, and the prednisone dose was tapered over 3 months. She underwent physical therapy twice weekly and was advised to take oral calcium (1000 mg daily) and vitamin D (1000 IU daily) due to concerns about adverse effects on bone associated with steroid use and to use contraception due to potential teratogenicity of methotrexate. At most recent follow-up 6 months after initial presentation, the skin tightening on her bilateral forearms and shins had decreased and her hand and elbow mobility had improved, but the groove sign on the right forearm persisted.

scenario: A 52-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with 3 days of headache, fatigue, and expressive aphasia. She did not take medications, supplements, or illicit substances. She was afebrile, with blood pressure of 232/133 mm Hg and heart rate of 86/min. She had expressive aphasia and confusion but no other neurologic abnormalities. Laboratory values included platelet count 35 000/μL (reference, 150 000-450 000/μL); haptoglobin level, 20 mg/dL (reference, 41-165 mg/dL); lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level, 962 U/L (16.07 μkat/L) (reference, 140-280 U/L [2.34-4.68 μkat/L]); creatinine level, 1.44 mg/dL (127.3 μmol/L) (reference, 0.6-1.1 mg/dL [53.04-97.24 μmol/L]); total bilirubin, 2.7 mg/dL (46.18 μmol/L) (reference, 0.1-1.2 mg/dL [1.71-20.52 μmol/L]); indirect bilirubin, 1.6 mg/dL (27.37 μmol/L) (reference, 0.2-0.8 mg/dL [3.42-13.68 μmol/L]); and fibrinogen, 420 mg/dL (reference, 200-400 mg/dL). Hemoglobin level, mean corpuscular volume, international normalized ratio, vitamin B12level, and thyrotropin level were normal. A peripheral blood smear showed 1 schistocyte per high-power field (Figure). PLASMIC score was 5, consistent with a 6% risk of immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (iTTP). A sample for disintegrin and metalloprotease with thrombospondin type 1 repeats-13 (ADAMTS13) activity was sent. Testing for HIV, CMV, HCV, Lyme ELISA, ANA, dsDNA, and Coombs test were normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the brain showed diffuse cerebral edema without ischemia or mass effect. She was treated with intravenous nicardipine for hypertensive emergency. Her blood pressure declined to 128/76 mm Hg and her expressive aphasia resolved, but she remained confused, with poor insight and diminished attention. On hospital day 4, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed numerous multifocal infarctions, ADAMTS13 activity was 6% (normal, ≥61%) with an inhibitor titer of 2.9 Bethesda units (reference, ≤0.4), and her peripheral blood smear showed 5 schistocytes per high-power field (Figure). Hemoglobin level was 9.3 g/dL; platelet count, 65 000 cells/μL; haptoglobin level, less than 20 mg/dL; and LDH level, 597 U/L (9.97 μkat/L).

options.B: Start daily therapeutic plasma exchange and methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days
