Patients who were treated with radiotherapy and an alkylating agent before age 1 year, as with this patient, may have up to 3.8 times greater risk of developing LMS.4 Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor that is typically found in the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, retroperitoneum, limbs, uterus, and pelvis of patients with retinoblastoma.3Leiomyosarcoma of large blood vessels comprises approximately 2% of LMS and is often found in the inferior vena cava, femoral, saphenous, jugular, or iliac veins.5 Prognosis is based on histologic grade, tumor size, and tumor depth.6Extrauterine LMS has a 40% 5-year risk of recurrence following resection, and for uterine LMS, the recurrence rates are as high as 70%.6To our knowledge, there are few studies to guide optimal treatment of early-stage disease. Surgical resection is the standard for local disease, and offers a chance at a cure with R0 resection.6Adjuvant radiotherapy in early-stage disease has been shown to decrease the risk of local recurrence; however, a recent large, randomized clinical trial of patients with retroperitoneal LMS demonstrated a limited utility of adjuvant radiotherapy.6,7Adjuvant chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes for patients with uterine LMS.8There have been studies that attempt to risk stratify and identify patients with nonuterine LMS who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy; however, these patients are part of broader studies on the treatment of STS and those with LMS are not the primary study population.6,9There are few data on advanced LMS, although most first-line regimens tend to include doxorubicin-based therapy.6 This patient’s case was discussed among the tumor board and given positive margins and a high-grade pathology; she received adjuvant proton radiotherapy to the margin edge with close monitoring for recurrence. This case reflects the importance of close monitoring of patients with a history of hereditary retinoblastoma, with a particular emphasis on screening for bone and STS as well as melanoma. Current expert recommendation includes an annual physical examination at a long-term survivor clinic, patient education, and consideration of screening whole-body magnetic resonance imaging.10

scenario: A 53-year-old man received a diagnosis of stage IV melanoma with metastatic disease to the spine and brain 3 months before presentation. Four weeks following receipt of immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab, he developed acute abdominal pain in the setting of a rapidly rising lactic acid dehydrogenase levels, prompting hospital admission. Imaging results showed mild disease progression (new ascites and periportal metabolic lymph node). Splenic infarct and portal/splenic vein thrombi were identified as etiologies of his acute pain and were presumed to be secondary to hypercoagulable state of malignancy. Over the next 3 days, he had rising serum creatinine (sCr) levels (baseline, approximately 1 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4]). The initial workup included ultrasonography and urinalysis. Ultrasonography results showed abnormal intraparenchymal flow to both kidneys without evidence of kidney artery stenosis. Urine studies were consistent with prerenal etiology, while the presence of casts suggested acute tubular necrosis. Nephrotoxic medications (omeprazole/pantoprazole) were discontinued. The top differential diagnoses at this juncture included contrast-induced nephropathy or immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)–induced acute interstitial nephritis, and empirical high dose steroids were prescribed. Despite observation and steroid treatment, his sCr levels continued to increase over the next 5 days, peaking at 5.8 mg/dL, and the patient progressed into anuric kidney failure, requiring hemodialysis. This prompted a kidney biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Figure). One week later, he received encorafenib, aBRAFinhibitor.1Two weeks later, the patient’s kidney function began to improve, and hemodialysis was discontinued. He continued to show gradual improvement, with a return to near baseline kidney function (sCr level, 1.3 mg/dL) approximately 6 weeks after treatment initiation.

options.A: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
options.C: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis

answer: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis
distractors: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. Although contrast can induce ATN, the peak in sCr levels typically occurs acutely after exposure (within 48-72 hours).9However, this patient was in the hospital for several weeks, with no improvement in sCr levels until after encorafenib was administered. The patient’s other nephrotoxic exposures included proton-pump inhibitors, which are associated with allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN) rather than ATN.10 While AIN secondary to ICI therapy was also in the differential, there was no patchy edema or inflammatory cell infiltrate on pathology to support this diagnosis. Although histopathologic findings may have been affected by the course of steroids, the patient’s concomitant rapidly worsening kidney function made a diagnosis of AIN unlikely. Finally, albeit the exhaustive sampling of the biopsy cores was per protocol, there was no histopathologic evidence of microthrombi or postinfectious glomerulonephritis. This case illustrates a rare finding of metastatic melanoma with glomerular involvement followed by anuric kidney failure from ATN, with substantial recovery of kidney function with encorafenib. In conclusion, kidney metastases should be considered in patients with advanced melanoma who present with kidney failure, even if there is no visible mass on imaging. Kidney biopsy and/or treatment targeted at melanoma cells may be appropriate steps in management.

scenario: A White woman in her late 50s with a medical history of osteoporosis, hyperlipidemia, and migraines presented with hematuria. Results of computed tomography (CT) imaging showed an 8×6×5-cm right kidney lesion (Figure 1, A). The patient underwent surgical resection with a right nephrectomy and an apparent diagnosis of angiomyolipoma (AML). One year later, the patient underwent excision of a right iliac wing lesion, and pathologic findings demonstrated xanthoma of bone with sclerosis. Three years after this second surgery, she presented with new abdominal pain. Results of CT imaging revealed a 4.3-cm retrocaval mass at the level of the renal right vein. She underwent surgical resection, and results of pathologic evaluation were consistent with the original tumor. Follow-up CT imaging revealed a 1.2-cm left upper lobe lung nodule and a 0.8-cm right upper lobe lung nodule, as well as a pulmonary embolism and a left 6th rib fracture. These lesions were fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography avid. The patient denied constitutional symptoms such as fatigue, fever, chills, and night sweats. She underwent bilateral video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery wedge resections of the lung lesions, which were also consistent with the primary tumor. Five years later, the patient (now in her late 60s) presented with multiple left pleural-based lung lesions (Figure 1, B). Results of all laboratory testing were within reference ranges. These pleural-based lesions were resected with left video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery partial pleurectomy, and results of pathologic evaluation were positive for HMB45 and Melan-A.
explanation: This patient has metastatic epithelioid angiomyolipoma (EAML), an unusual variant of AML, which is among the most commonly encountered types of kidney masses. The resected masses were consistent with an epithelioid mesenchymal neoplasm with clear cell morphology having low to intermediate grade features (low mitotic rate with focal tumor necrosis;Figure 2). The diagnosis of EAML was confirmed with HMB45 and Melan-A staining. Perivascular epithelioid cell neoplasms (PEComas) is a family of related mesenchymal tumors, including AML, lymphangiomyomatosis, clear cell tumors of the lung, and rare morphologically and immunophenotypically similar tumors.1These tumors are defined by perivascular epithelioid cells or spindle cells with clear eosinophilic cytoplasm and are typically arranged around blood vessels with immunoreactivity to smooth muscle and melanocytic (HMB5 and Melan-A) markers.2Typically, PEComa tumors occur at visceral, retroperitoneal, and abdominopelvic sites (the uterus being the most common site)3and are rarely malignant (only 6% to 7% demonstrate distant metastasis).1 A subset of PEComa tumors includes AMLs, which are the most frequent benign kidney tumor, have a prevalence of 0.2% to 0.6%, have a strong female predilection, and occur as sporadic isolated entities in 80% of cases.4A distinct subset are EAMLs, distinguished by the presence of smooth muscle markers (caldesmon and smooth muscle actin) as well as melanocytic markers.4These tumors are described as a malignant neoplasm with distant metastasis in one-third of patients and with metastasis more common for patients with marked nuclear atypia or necrosis.1These tumors are associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) variations leading to mTOR pathway activation.5Approximately 80% of patients with kidney EAML have autosomal dominant germline variations inTSC1orTSC2gene; however, only 5% to 10% of patients have tuberous sclerosis disease. Imaging and differentiation of EAML from renal cell carcinoma can be challenging, but new magnetic resonance imaging modalities help to differentiate these tumor types.6 Treatment strategies for this disease process include active surveillance for small asymptomatic masses. Symptomatic masses and masses greater than 4 cm should be treated with radical or partial nephrectomy or ablative therapy.7For patients with metastatic disease, treatment with mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus is often beneficial. A phase 2 registration trial8studied response to nab-sirolimus and found that median progression-free survival was 8.9 months, with response depending onTSCgene variation—100% of patients withTSC2variation had a partial response vs 20% of those withTSC1variation and 9% of those without aTSCgene variation. Another study estimated that distant metastasis occurs 1.5 years to 9 years postoperatively, with death within 1 year of metastasis.9Limited data exist on the benefit of surgical management for distant metastasis in EAML. This patient underwent initial therapy with radical nephrectomy followed by therapy with mTOR inhibition at the time of metastatic diagnosis. She subsequently underwent multiple surgeries to remove oligometastases. This case illustrates the use of oligometastatic resection for minimization of tumor burden as an overall strategy to preemptively palliate expected symptom(s) and translate to longer overall survival. Additionally, a surgical strategy secondarily provides tumor tissue that can be genotyped for further research efforts.

caption: A sagittal magnetic resonance imaging scan with contrast shows areas of metastatic breast cancer to the lumbar vertebral bodies, and the arrowheads show leptomeningeal spread.
scenario: A 39-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer treated with anti-ERBB2 (formerly HER2) chemotherapy (ado-trastuzumab emtansine) presented to the emergency department with acute onset paralysis. Earlier that day she had upper-back muscle spasms while gardening. A few hours later, she developed weakness of both hands and legs, followed by urinary retention and saddle anesthesia. On arrival to the emergency department, the patient was febrile but hemodynamically stable. On physical examination, she had areflexia and weakness affecting all 4 limbs, with a sensory deficit distal to the T4 dermatome. Proprioception and vibratory sensation were intact throughout. Speech, comprehension, and cranial nerves were intact. Laboratory test results revealed elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, including white and red blood cell counts, protein and glucose levels, infectious studies, and cytologic testing, was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the total spine showed vertebral body metastases unchanged from a computed tomography scan obtained 8 months prior (Figure 1), multiple areas of new leptomeningeal enhancement around the distal spinal cord, and tumor infiltration of multiple vertebral bodies. An electromyogram showed grossly preserved motor conduction in the upper and lower extremities. F wave latencies (a measure of nerve conduction velocity between the spine and limb) were undetectable in the upper extremities and were normal in the lower extremities, suggesting upper motor neuron disease. Sensory conduction amplitudes of upper and lower extremity peripheral nerves were mildly decreased.
explanation: Spinal cord infarct is a devastating syndrome characterized by abrupt symptom onset and accounts for 5% to 8% of acute myelopathy.1At presentation, 72% of patients with spinal cord infarct have associated back or limb pain at the level of involvement. This patient lost motor function and reflexes at the level of the infarct (C6 and C7) and had a loss of sensation at T4, but proprioception and vibratory sensation were maintained throughout the spine. These are hallmark examination findings of disruption of the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior (but not posterior) spinal columns. The cervical plexus (C1 through C4) likely provided redundant innervation to the patient’s upper trunk, accounting for the T4 sensory deficit distal to the infarct. Only 24% of patients with spinal cord infarct have an abnormal MRI at the time of presentation, with most infarctions appearing as myelomalacia (radiographic “softening” of the spinal cord) on subsequent imaging (Figure 2).2Spinal cord infarct is thus largely a clinical diagnosis. Although more typically a result of a perioperative complication, this patient’s anterior spinal artery was likely disrupted by either direct invasion by breast cancer or by a thromboembolic event. Spinal cord infarct is treated with supportive care and reversal of the inciting process when possible. This patient was treated with oral and intrathecal chemotherapy, anticoagulation, and physical therapy; she had modest improvement in strength during a 2-month period. Spinal cord infarct has an estimated 3-year mortality rate of 23% and a wheelchair dependence rate of 42%.3 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired autoimmune peripheral demyelinating disease. This uncommon syndrome (incidence of 1 to 2 per 100 000 people) can be triggered by infection and hematologic cancer.4Weakness owing to GBS progresses over weeks in an ascending fashion, with absent deep tendon reflexes seen in virtually all patients. Cerebrospinal fluid cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevation of protein level with normal white blood cell count) is present in approximately two-thirds of patients with GBS and may take 1 week to develop. Although this patient was areflexic, the acute onset of her symptoms and preserved motor conduction on electromyogram do not support a diagnosis of GBS. Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is found at autopsy in 20% of patients with metastatic cancer, and breast cancer is the solid tumor most likely to spread to the leptomeninges.5Multiple areas of involvement are common, and presenting symptoms, which correspond to areas of spinal involvement, are often heterogenous and multifocal. Spine MRI is 76% sensitive for the detection of LMD, demonstrating enhancement of the spinal cord or cauda equina.6Cerebrospinal fluid cytologic testing is only 54% sensitive with the first sample; however, only 3% of patients with LMD have completely normal CSF.7Common CSF findings include elevated protein level, decreased glucose level, and white blood cell pleocytosis (most commonly lymphocytosis). Although this patient had leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI, these areas did not correspond to her upper extremity neurologic deficits. The unremarkable CSF analysis further excluded paralysis owing to LMD. Although few medications are associated with acute onset quadriparesis, it is important to be mindful of potential drug adverse effects in patients with cancer. Adverse effects associated with ado-trastuzumab emtansine could explain some of the findings in this case, including peripheral neuropathy (shown on electromyogram) and muscle pain, but not paralysis.

caption: A, A July 2020 gallium 68 dotatate positron emission tomography–computed tomography image shows extensive but stable disease from the patient’s metastatic neuroendocrine tumor (NET). Each hyperdense area, except the physiologic uptake in the pituitary gland and bladder (arrowheads), corresponds to a NET deposit. B and C, Photomicrographs from the bone marrow biopsy specimen show the presence of tumor cells (arrowheads) staining strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin (original magnification ×20).
scenario: A 72-year-old woman with metastatic, well-differentiated, small intestinal neuroendocrine tumor (NET) presented for routine follow-up in September 2020 with worsening fatigue and flushing. She was initially diagnosed with metastatic involvement of the liver, bone, and intra-abdominal lymph nodes in 2015 and received 3 treatments with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) in 2017. After 2 years of disease stability she was retreated with PRRT in November 2019 because of radiographic progression of disease and worsening symptoms. A third dose of PRRT was given in March 2020; a fourth was deferred owing to persistent thrombocytopenia after treatment. Gallium 68 dotatate positron emission tomography–computed tomography in July 2020 revealed stable disease (Figure, A). Laboratory results from the clinic visit noted a hemoglobin level of 7.5 g/dL (red cell distribution width, 63.2 fL), platelet count of 54 ×103/μL, and absolute neutrophil count of 1310/μL. (To convert hemoglobin to grams per liter, multiply by 10; platelet and absolute neutrophil counts to ×109/L, by 0.001.) Results of a peripheral blood smear did not suggest the presence of circulating blasts or schistocytes. She was referred to the hematologic malignancies clinic for evaluation. An extensive laboratory workup assessing nutritional deficiencies, viral exposure, and autoimmune disease was unrevealing. Hematopathology slides of a subsequent bone marrow biopsy specimen revealed tumor cells staining strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin (Figure, B) and chromogranin (Figure, C).

options.B: Temporary myelosuppression from peptide receptor radionuclide therapy
options.C: Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow

answer: Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow
distractors: Temporary myelosuppression from peptide receptor radionuclide therapy
explanation: C. Neuroendocrine tumor infiltration of bone marrow Hematopathologic analysis revealed a mildly hypocellular marrow (10%-20% cellularity) with erythroid predominant trilineage hematopoiesis. No overt morphologic dysplasia or blasts were recognized; however, multiple aggregates of tumor cells that stained strongly positive by immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and chromogranin were noted, which confirmed metastatic involvement of the NET in the bone marrow. Reports of bone marrow metastases from well-differentiated NETs are rare; we found only 5 cases in the literature since 2009.1Patients with solid tumor metastases to bone marrow typically present with thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated red cell distribution width and carry a poor prognosis.2For this patient, extensive bone involvement from her NET may have predisposed her to develop bone marrow infiltration; this association, however, has not been described in patients with NET and diffuse bone metastases. Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) is a devastating but infrequent complication of PRRT. The incidence of t-MDS with PRRT is estimated to be 2% to 5%, with a median time to onset after the completion of treatment from 12 to 78 months.3Potential risk factors that predispose patients with NETs to t-MDS, such as use of alkylating agents, presence of bone metastases, and prior exposure to ionizing radiation, have been inconsistently implicated across studies.4Patients with certain somatic mutations or clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential may be more inclined to develop t-MDS after PRRT; however, this association remains understudied.5There does not appear to be a dose effect; patients receiving retreatment with PRRT do not appear to have increased incidence of t-MDS compared with PRRT-naive patients.6The prognosis of patients who develop t-MDS is dismal, with median overall survival times just beyond 1 year from the time of diagnosis.3 Hematologic toxic effects of PRRT are typically subacute and reversible. In the randomized NETTER-1 study,7which garnered PRRT its approval for patients with progressive gastroenteropancreatic NETs, the most frequent grade 3 and 4 hematologic adverse events (AEs) were lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in 9%, 2%, and 1% of cases, respectively.7None of the hematologic AEs were permanent. In a large observational cohort study of more than 600 patients with gastroenteropancreatic and bronchial NETs who underwent PRRT, 10% of patients experienced grade 3 or 4 hematologic AEs.8The most common of these AEs were thrombocytopenia (5% of cases), leukopenia (5%), and anemia (4%). Within 3 months of follow-up, 77% of these AEs resolved. Some cohort studies, however, suggest that hematologic AEs experienced by patients during PRRT can take longer to resolve.9 Aplastic anemia, characterized by a loss of hematopoietic stem cells, typically occurs because of toxins, viral syndromes, immune destruction, or underlying genetic syndromes.10Marrow toxic agents include some antimicrobial therapies (eg, chloramphenicol), chemotherapy, or high doses of ionizing radiation. Although this patient received ionizing radiation via PRRT, her bone marrow had only mild hypocellularity and no dysplastic features. In the setting of progressive disease, absence of other cytoreductive options and high tumor programmed death-ligand 1 expression, the patient began immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab. Her anemia and thrombocytopenia are being managed with regular transfusions while disease response reassessment is pending.

caption: A, Computed tomography scan showing symmetrical enlargement of both psoas muscles (arrowheads). B and C, Magnetic resonance images showing edema in both psoas muscles and peripheral contrast enhancement of the fascia, with arrowheads pointing to the imaging abnormalities.
scenario: A 39-year-old female patient with alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma and bone metastases presented in April 2020 with lower back pain, which was aggravated while standing and walking. She reported no known trauma, and no motor or sensory deficits were noted during clinical examination. She had no fever. After the initial sarcoma diagnosis in September 2018, the patient received 8 cycles of doxorubicin hydrochloride and ifosfamide along with regional hyperthermia, followed by good tumor response. The patient had a history of a pathological fracture of L4, which had been treated with radiotherapy and vertebroplasty in November 2019 and remained unchanged on imaging obtained in April 2020. The treatment regimen recently had been switched to gemcitabine hydrochloride and docetaxel in January 2020 following osseous progression during maintenance chemotherapy with trofosfamide, idarubicin hydrochloride, and etoposide. On restaging computed tomography, symmetrical enlargement of both psoas muscles was observed with intramuscular hypodensity (Figure, A). The patient reported lower back pain but no motor or sensory deficits. Further workup with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed extensive, nearly symmetrical swelling in both psoas muscles and sharply delineated, peripheral contrast enhancement of the fascia with strict horizontal bounds (Figure, B and C).
explanation: Radiation recall is a rare diagnosis in which inflammatory reactions are induced by chemotherapeutic agents in previously irradiated tissues. D’Angio et al1were the first to describe this phenomenon in 1959. In pediatric and adult patients treated first with radiotherapy and then with intravenous administration of actinomycin D, development of erythema was observed and was sharply limited to prior irradiation fields in the course of actinomycin D treatment. Since publication of the study by D’Angio et al,1many cytotoxic agents have been identified as potential triggers for radiation recall events. Among the most frequent drugs associated with these events are anthracyclines and taxanes, such as docetaxel.2In recent years, gemcitabine also was implicated in several cases.3Although radiation recall was initially and most often reported to affect the skin, such reactions associated with use of gemcitabine predominantly seem to be associated with inflammation of internal tissues, especially muscles, triggering radiation recall myositis.4-6 Radiation recall events typically occur days to weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy but have been reported up to 15 years after radiotherapy treatment.7The underlying mechanisms of these events have not yet been elucidated. Distinct mechanisms of action have been proposed because various cytotoxic agents have been associated with this adverse event. These mechanisms include alterations of pharmacodynamics based on abnormal intracellular expression and activity of proteins attributable to radiotherapy-induced injury of exposed tissues and idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reactions.2 No strict treatment recommendations for radiation recall myositis are available.6Corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can alleviate symptoms, and discontinuation of the chemotherapeutic agent may be considered depending on clinical severity.8 The patient in this study developed radiation recall myositis triggered by docetaxel and gemcitabine hydrochloride, 2 agents associated with this adverse effect. This condition occurred 5 months after the last course of radiotherapy (total dose: 40 Gy for L4 and 35 Gy for the left tenth rib; ray type: 10 MeV; radiotherapy technique: volumetric modulated arc therapy) and 2 months after commencement of chemotherapy. Besides myositis of both psoas muscles (Figure), the autochthonous back muscles and the intercostal muscles around the left tenth rib, which previously had also been irradiated, also showed signs of myositis on MRI. The extent of myositis reached beyond the 50% isodose line of the radiotherapy plans. There was no diffusion restriction of these lesions observed on MRI, and together with nonelevated C-reactive protein and the absence of fever in the patient, an infectious cause seemed unlikely. Docetaxel and gemcitabine treatments were discontinued, and the patient began taking high-dose prednisone, followed by rapid elimination of the lower back pain. The diagnosis of radiation recall myositis can be challenging if the medical history and treatment timelines are not available in sufficient detail. Characteristic imaging findings may help in identifying a diagnosis, yet they have to be put into context of the patient’s history. Normal inflammatory markers in the blood and the absence of imaging signs of abscess or hematoma help in narrowing down the diagnosis. In the literature, no specific relationship between radiotherapy dose and occurrence of recall myositis has been established. Moreover, no typical temporal association has been identified so far. Oncologists, radiation oncologists, and imaging specialists should be aware of radiation recall myositis to differentiate it from other causes and to ensure timely management of this adverse effect.

caption: A, Clinical image of petechial eruption on the scalp. B, Punch biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A man in his 60s presented to the clinic with a several-day history of nontender, nonitchy purpuric rash on his scalp. The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). A punch biopsy specimen from the scalp was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B).
explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

caption: Skin lesions on the patient with widespread, erythematous, indurated nodules involving his head and neck (A) and trunk (B). C, Histologic findings demonstrate diffuse dermal infiltrates, extending to the subcutis, with sparing of the upper papillary dermis (original magnification ×20). The infiltrates are characterized by immature myeloid cells (inset, original magnification ×400).
scenario: A 29-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of rapidly growing, widespread, asymptomatic skin nodules all over his body. He denied having fever, chills, fatigue, night sweats, or weight loss. He had no history of malignant neoplasm or chemical exposure. Physical examination findings demonstrated numerous erythematous, indurated nodules involving the surface of his head, neck, torso, and extremities, without ulceration or scarring (Figure, A and B). Findings of systemic reviews were unremarkable, and there was no lymphadenopathy or peripheral nerve enlargement. Complete blood cell count with differential results were normal (white blood cell count, 6060/μL, normal range, 4500-10 000/μL; absolute neutrophils, 3070/μL, normal range, 1800-8300/μL [to convert cell counts to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]). Serum lactate dehydrogenase level was elevated (279 U/L, normal range, 100-240 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]). Biopsies from skin nodules (Figure, C) and bone marrow were obtained.
explanation: A. Aleukemic cutaneous myeloid sarcoma Skin biopsy results revealed diffuse, nonepidermotropic infiltrate of atypical mononuclear cells involving the entire dermis and extending to the subcutis (Figure, C). The infiltrating cells were medium sized, round to oval, with slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and distinct oval-shaped or kidney-shaped basophilic nuclei. They stained positively for CD45, MPO, KP-1, and CD43 and were negative for CD3, CD123, CD20, CD34, CD56, CD117, and CD138, compatible with primitive myeloid cells. Mitotic figures were noted. Bone marrow biopsy results showed no evidence of leukemic involvement. Results of subsequent fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis performed on paraffin sections of the skin biopsy did not reveal 11q23/MLL rearrangement or t(8;21)(q22;q22.1) rearrangement. NeitherNPM1norFLT3variation was detected in the skin lesion. Myeloid sarcoma (also known as extramedullary myeloid tumor or granulocytic sarcoma) is characterized by leukemic cells of a myeloid lineage infiltrating an extramedullary location and typically occurs in the following settings: as a forerunner of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in patients without leukemia, as the acute leukemic progression of myelodysplastic syndrome or blast crisis in chronic myeloid leukemia, or as relapse of antecedent AML.1-3It has been reported at nearly every anatomic site and is most frequently encountered in the skin and soft tissues, lymph nodes, and gastrointestinal tract.4When the leukemia cells infiltrate specifically in the skin, cutaneous myeloid sarcoma has been referred to as leukemia cutis. There is a wide age distribution; however, myeloid sarcoma appears to be more common in the pediatric age group, with an incidence of up to 30% in children with AML vs 2% to 5% in adults.4,5 Leukemia may manifest in the skin as a leukemid reaction or, less commonly, as cutaneous myeloid sarcoma. Leukemids represent nonspecific changes in the skin and most commonly result from bone marrow failure or humoral response to the primary tumor.1In contrast, cutaneous myeloid sarcoma denotes the specific infiltration of neoplastic myeloid cells.1It presents as multiple papules, plaques, or nodules with a characteristic reddish-brown or violaceous color. The most commonly involved region is the torso, although the head and neck regions and the extremities, as well as the mucosal region, can also be involved.5Skin manifestation without evidence of systemic disease is referred to as aleukemic cutaneous myeloid sarcoma, but its presence is sufficient to establish a clinical diagnosis of AML. Previous studies have suggested that bone marrow involvement would become detectable in nearly all patients, with a mean interval of 10 months.5 Recognition of this cutaneous phenomenon remains important for further classification and early diagnosis of myeloid leukemia. Nevertheless, diagnosis is often difficult owing to the presentation of isolated cutaneous findings outside the context of systemic disease.1Histologically, cutaneous lesions show diffuse or nodular dermal infiltrates, with sparing of the upper papillary dermis. Involvement of the subcutis is common. Prominent single files of neoplastic cells between collagen bundles can be observed. The infiltrate is composed of immature myeloid cells. Markers usually expressed include CD45, CD68, and MPO. Lysozyme, CD34, CD13, CD14, CD15, and CD33 are positive in a variety of diseases.6Few data on cytogenetic abnormalities in cutaneous myeloid sarcoma are available. The t(8;21)(q22;q22.1) and 11q23 abnormalities are the most commonly reported chromosomal abnormalities in myeloid sarcoma.7Variations inNPM1andFLT3have been reported in 14% and 15% of patients with myeloid sarcoma, respectively.8,9 Skin and bone marrow histologic findings are critical to confirm the diagnosis. Monomorphic skin lesions and the absence of peripheral nerve enlargement exclude lepromatous leprosy. Sarcoidosis can be considered but is less likely because of the fast growth of the skin nodules. Cutaneous lymphoma usually presents as polymorphic skin lesions, including irregular patches, plaques, and tumors. Expression of myeloid markers by the infiltrating cells helps to rule out cutaneous lymphoma. Patients with aleukemic cutaneous myeloid sarcoma should be managed in the same way as patients with bone marrow involvement. Outcomes are usually poor, although they may be slightly better than outcomes of primary or relapsed AML without extramedullary involvement.5This patient was treated with 7 cycles of chemotherapy using hyperfractionated cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone (known as hyper-CVAD) regimens. He had been in remission for 2 years at the time of last follow-up. This case highlights the importance of establishing the diagnosis of cutaneous myeloid sarcoma because it is considered a bone marrow equivalent to the diagnosis of AML.

caption: External slitlamp photograph of the right eye with magnified iris lesion (blue arrowheads) (A) and fundus photograph of the right eye (B).
scenario: A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

options.A: Ask about low back pain and order HLA-B27 testing
options.B: Ask about oral ulcers and perform fluorescein angiography
options.C: Ask about tattoos and order chest computed tomography to evaluate for lymphadenopathy
options.D: Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED

answer: Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED
distractors: Ask about low back pain and order HLA-B27 testing
Ask about oral ulcers and perform fluorescein angiography
Ask about tattoos and order chest computed tomography to evaluate for lymphadenopathy
explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

caption: A, The anterior segment of the right eye revealed a clear cornea, iris with an ectropion uvea, prominent vascularization, and an irregularly shaped pupil, (arrowheads). The lens exhibited a posterior subcapsular cataract. B, Examination of the posterior pole demonstrated a triangular-shaped fold in the macula, accompanied by diffuse, shallow subretinal fluid (arrowheads).
scenario: An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

options.A: Return to the operating room immediately for retained PFO removal
options.B: Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities
options.C: Return later for secondary lens placement with concurrent PFO removal
options.D: Initiate corticosteroid drops to aid PFO absorption

answer: Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities
distractors: Return to the operating room immediately for retained PFO removal
Return later for secondary lens placement with concurrent PFO removal
Initiate corticosteroid drops to aid PFO absorption
explanation: Retained PFO in the vitreous and subretinal space after retinal surgery B. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

caption: A, External photograph at first presentation demonstrating an inferonasal granular white opacity without overlying epithelial defect, deep vessels in the corneal stroma, and associated corneal thickening. B, Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) showing hyperreflective infiltrate in the area of the corneal opacity with associated corneal thickening.
scenario: A 74-year-old man was referred for evaluation of suspected interstitial keratitis of the right eye. He noted progressive blurry vision but denied eye pain or antecedent trauma. Visual acuity on presentation was 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed a 5-mm inferonasal granular white opacity in the anterior corneal stroma without overlying epithelial defect. There were deep vessels visible in the anterior corneal stroma and Descemet membrane folds (Figure 1A). The remainder of the anterior segment was unremarkable. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated a hyperreflective infiltrate in the area of the corneal opacity with associated corneal thickening (Figure 1B). Dilated fundus examination did not reveal any vitritis or retinal findings. Examination of the left eye was unremarkable. Medical history was remarkable for a 10–pack-year smoking history, stable thoracic aortic aneurysm, and hypertension. There was no history of contact lens wear. A review of systems was negative for a history of eye infections, travel outside of the US, or hearing changes. Limited workup was positive for herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) and HSV2 immunoglobulin G (IgG) and negative for antinuclear antibody (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), rapid plasma reagin (RPR), anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP), and interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis. Given the positive HSV1 and HSV2 IgG and unremarkable preliminary autoimmune and infectious workup, the patient was given topical corticosteroids and oral valaciclovir for presumed herpetic interstitial keratitis.1,2His corneal opacity persisted despite this treatment.

options.B: Refer to rheumatology for additional autoimmune workup

distractors: Refer to rheumatology for additional autoimmune workup
explanation: C. Perform a corneal biopsy Corneal scraping and culture were not performed, given the intact corneal epithelium and lack of antecedent trauma or pain (option D). Given positive HSV antibodies and negative ANCA, ANA, and anti-CCP, there was low suspicion for an autoimmune etiology, and referral to rheumatology was deferred (option B). A diagnostic anterior chamber paracentesis was not performed, given the lack of anterior chamber inflammation (option A). A corneal biopsy was performed (option C), which showed a few keratinocytes as well as corneal edema and inflammation without deposits, granulomatous inflammation, or infectious organisms. The patient continued topical corticosteroids. Despite treatment, the patient re-presented with necrotizing scleritis and anterior segment neovascularization (Figure 2). Broad additional workups were performed in conjunction with rheumatology, including 2 additional corneal and scleral biopsies (without evidence of amyloid, infection, or neoplasia), erythrocyte sedimentation rate/C-reactive protein, fluorescein angiogram, carotid ultrasound (to evaluate for ocular ischemic syndrome), corneal scraping and culture, and hepatitis and HIV serologies, all of which were unrevealing, and the sclerokeratitis was attributed to an undifferentiated autoimmune process. Over the course of the next few months, the patient was stabilized receiving high-dose oral prednisone and rituximab. Eight months after initial presentation, visual acuity acutely worsened to light perception, and the patient developed a new afferent pupillary defect in the right eye with ptosis and limitations in upgaze and adduction. Magnetic resonance imaging at that time demonstrated asymmetric enhancement of the tendinous portion of the right inferior rectus. B-scan ultrasound was remarkable for choroidal effusions with overlying retinal detachment. He underwent biopsy of the sclera and orbit, which, along with genetic sequencing, revealed conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma (Figure 2, inset). After diagnosis, the original sclerocorneal biopsy underwent additional sectioning, and a single distal section with a few atypical cells was detected. These stained positive for p40, which was also expressed in the tumor. This case represents a rare presentation of conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma, masquerading as interstitial keratitis. Previously termed mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the ocular surface, conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma, this tumor falls under the headingocular surface squamous cell neoplasia(OSSN).3This tumor is relatively rare, and to our knowledge, this was the first case of the tumor masquerading as interstitial keratitis.4There have been a few reports of OSSN masquerading as sclerokeratitis.5Interestingly, the majority of these cases, including the one case of OSSN presenting as interstitial keratitis, were definitively diagnosed as squamous cell carcinoma on the first biopsy.5-9 The patient’s immunosuppression was stopped, and the case was presented to tumor board. Orbital exenteration was recommended given the orbital extension of the malignancy, followed by intensity-modulated radiation therapy and adjuvant immunotherapy. The patient continues to have close follow-up for the first 2 years to monitor for recurrence, and recently, a metastasis to the abdominal muscles was discovered.10This case demonstrates the importance of revisiting a broad differential diagnosis if the disease is unresponsive to conventional therapy and the importance of communication with pathology, including requesting additional sectioning in atypical cases.

caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
scenario: A 37-year-old woman with a history of resolved nasopharyngeal carcinoma presented with transient binocular horizontal diplopia for 2 years. She received chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, along with radiotherapy (70 Gy in 33 fractions), which was completed 9 years earlier. Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). The movements of the other extraocular muscles showed a full range of motion, with no nystagmus or involuntary contractions similar to those of the right lateral rectus muscle. Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.

options.D: Reevaluate with MRI of the brain and orbit in 6 months

distractors: Reevaluate with MRI of the brain and orbit in 6 months
explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

caption: Red-free fundus photographs demonstrating large serous detachments and deep subretinal lesions (arrowheads) with optical coherence tomography B-scan confirming the detachment. A, Right eye. B, Left eye.
scenario: A 19-year-old man was referred for evaluation of bilateral retinal detachments. His visual acuity with correction on a Snellen chart was 20/400 and 20/500 in the right and left eyes, respectively. Anterior examination revealed no anterior chamber cells and well-dilated iris with clear lens in both eyes. Posterior examination showed no vitreous cells, hyperemic and elevated discs, macular edema, and large inferior serous detachments with deep, creamy lesions throughout the posterior pole in both eyes (Figure). No retinal breaks were observed in either eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated subretinal and intraretinal fluid in the macula of both eyes, with a subfoveal bacillary detachment, ie, a splitting at the level of the inner segments of the photoreceptors. B-scan ultrasound confirmed retinal detachments in both eyes with no choroidal masses or detachment. Medical history included attention-deficit/hyperactive disorder, for which he took dextroamphetamine (Adderall) since childhood. The patient noted that vision was progressively worsening starting 1 week prior to presentation, during which time he was recovering from an upper respiratory tract illness and diarrhea that self-resolved. Review of systems was otherwise negative for any headache, altered mental status, chest pain, tinnitus, urinary issues, or trauma prior to presentation.

options.B: Send for infectious and inflammatory laboratory workup and start oral prednisone
options.C: Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel
options.D: Perform bilateral pars plana vitrectomy with or without scleral buckle for retinal detachment repair

answer: Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel
distractors: Send for infectious and inflammatory laboratory workup and start oral prednisone
Perform bilateral pars plana vitrectomy with or without scleral buckle for retinal detachment repair
explanation: C. Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel Following the patient’s initial presentation, he was found to have a blood pressure of 178/104. Basic laboratory work collected along with laboratory tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme with chest radiography were all negative except for a creatine level of 19.12 mg/dL. Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. Given the patient’s underlying etiology, immediate observation (answer A) or surgery (answer D) would not have been indicated. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. This case highlights the importance of systemic hypertension as a cause of bilateral serous retinal detachments, even in patients who are younger, previously healthy, and without more superficial signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Prompt workup and treatment are important to reduce the chance of short-term and long-term morbidity and mortality from uncontrolled hypertension.

caption: Slitlamp photograph of 2.5 × 3.0-mm nodule with telangiectasia 5 to 6 mm from the limbus, with a black arrowhead pointing to the nodule.
scenario: A 69-year-old female with a history of ulcerative colitis developed a bulbar conjunctival nodule in her left eye that was noted incidentally during an oculoplastic evaluation for dermatochalasis and eyelid herniation. She reported accompanying symptoms of bilateral eye fatigue, burning, and irritation. The patient did not report any other ocular symptoms. Visual acuity was 20/40 in the left eye and hand motion in the right eye due to a prior retinal detachment. A slitlamp examination revealed a 2.5 × 3.0-mm nodule with telangiectasia 5 to 6 mm from the limbus at the 10:00 position (Figure 1). No foreign body was found. The patient did not report fever, night sweats, or recent weight loss. Medical history was significant for ulcerative colitis, type 2 diabetes, gastroesophageal reflux disease, hypertension, and glaucoma in her right eye. At the time of presentation, her glaucoma was stable with intraocular pressure of 12 mm Hg in the right eye and 14 mm Hg in the left eye. Current medications included latanoprost nightly in her left eye and ophthalmic prednisone 2 to 3 times per day in her right eye. Family history was negative for cancer. Social history was notable for being from Durango, Mexico, and negative for smoking or alcohol.

options.D: Observe and follow up in 3 months

distractors: Observe and follow up in 3 months
explanation: C. Perform an excisional biopsy Excisional biopsy (C) is the optimal choice for this patient, as it allows for definitive histopathological examination of the nodule, particularly considering the patient’s history of ulcerative colitis and the presence of telangiectasia. Initiating topical mitomycin C (A) may be less appropriate, as it typically is used for confirmed ocular surface neoplasia, and using it without a definitive diagnosis could lead to inappropriate treatment and delay proper management. Starting systemic corticosteroids (B) usually is not ideal without clear evidence of systemic inflammation or an acute flare of ulcerative colitis and could mask the underlying condition. Finally, observing and following up in 3 months, while not an unreasonable option given the patient’s lack of symptoms, risks delaying the diagnosis of a potentially serious condition, such as a malignant neoplasm. Given the ease of an excisional biopsy and its ability to provide an immediate and accurate diagnosis, option C is likely the most appropriate approach. The biopsy revealed a monoclonal CD5+ small B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder, favoring small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry showed CD20+ cells with co-expression of CD5, CD43, and BCL2, and negative results for CD3, CD10, BCL1, and SOX11. CD23 expression was noted in rare cells. Ophthalmic adnexal lymphoma (OAL) is the most common malignant neoplasm involving the ocular adnexa and representing 11% to 24% of all ocular tumors. Primary OALs are rare, accounting for 8% of extranodal lymphomas, and as many as 20% primary conjunctival lymphomas may develop into systemic disease over time, although this may be months or even years later.1-3The most common subtypes include extranodal marginal zone lymphomas of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) (35%-80%), followed by follicular lymphoma (approximately 20%) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (approximately 8%).4Ocular adnexal SLL are rarer, with few reported cases.5,6 While less is known about ocular SLL specifically, predisposing factors for OAL, specifically MALT and DLBCL, include autoimmune conditions (eg, Sjögren syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease, systemic lupus erythematosus), immune deficiency or dysfunction, infectious etiologies (Chlamydiaspp andHelicobacter pylori), and prior radiation exposure.7-9This patient had a history of ulcerative colitis, which may bolster the link between autoimmune disease and conjunctival lymphoma. Treatment of OAL primarily depends on the extent of periocular or systemic involvement. For localized disease, complete surgical resection or external localized beam radiation therapy is often used. However, ocular SLL has an increased risk of extranodal metastases on presentation.5,6In these cases, therapy is not standardized; however, rituximab is commonly used, particularly if the tumor is large, infiltrative, and nonresectable. In our case, a complete excisional biopsy was performed with no evidence of recurrence. Nonetheless, long-term follow up is crucial, as patients with OAL and prior CLL or SLL demonstrated an increased incidence in both hematologic and solid secondary primary malignant neoplasms.10 Following a complete excisional biopsy, follow-up visits revealed no recurrence of ocular disease and good visual acuity (20/32) in the left eye. The patient was referred to hematology, and subsequent positron emission tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging orbits on last follow-up 8 months after excisional biopsy revealed no signs of systemic malignant neoplasm.

caption: A, Right eye fluorescein angiogram (FA) with insets of the computed tomography (CT) imaging of intracranial calcifications. B, Left eye fundus photograph with FA shown (lower left inset) and optical coherence tomography infrared image and B scan of chorioretinal lesions nasal to the optic nerve (lower right inset).
scenario: A 56-year-old female patient with type 2 diabetes presented to an emergency department with 3 days of syncope, headache, fatigue, myalgias, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed the following counts: protein, 0.095 g/dL (to convert protein to g/L, multiply by 10); glucose, 92 mg/dL (to convert glucose to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); white blood cells, 148/µL (to convert white blood cell count to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001); red blood cells, 0.000036 × 106/µL (to convert red blood cell count to × 1012/L, multiply by 1); neutrophils, 81% (to convert neutrophils to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01); and monocytes, 19% (to convert monocytes to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01). One week following admission, the patient reported floaters in her right eye with normal vision. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and scattered and linear formations of chorioretinal lesions with mild patchy venular staining, but no substantial leakage was observed on fluorescein angiography (FA) (Figure 1). Mild vitritis was observed in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the lesions nasal to the optic nerve in the left eye (Figure 1) showed retinal atrophy, retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy, and choroidal hyperreflectivity. Upon further questioning, she reported travel to Mexico in the last year. She denied eating undercooked meat, living in the Ohio River Valley, recent insect bites, exposure to cats, puppies, or lactating female dogs, or receiving immunocompromising or immunomodulating therapy.

options.A: Sulfamethoxazole, 800 mg, and trimethoprim, 160 mg, by mouth twice daily for 14 days
options.B: Serologic testing for antihelminth antibodies and inspection of stool for ova and parasites
options.C: Corticosteroids, 60 mg prednisone equivalent, by mouth daily

distractors: Sulfamethoxazole, 800 mg, and trimethoprim, 160 mg, by mouth twice daily for 14 days
Serologic testing for antihelminth antibodies and inspection of stool for ova and parasites
Corticosteroids, 60 mg prednisone equivalent, by mouth daily
explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV.
