explanation: This patient had new-onset right ptosis with an inability to elevate his right eye and abduct his left eye, with otherwise normal neurologic examination results. This combination of examination findings cannot be localized in the central nervous system, because there is involvement of the levator muscle and superior rectus on the right (innervated by cranial nerve III) and the lateral rectus on the left (innervated by cranial nerve VI). This should raise concern for ocular myasthenia gravis, and a readily accessible test in the clinic is an ice pack test or rest test, which should result in an improvement in the ptosis, as was seen in this patient. His palpebral fissure measured 1 mm before ice was applied and 6 mm 5 minutes after the application of ice. The ice test has been reported to have a sensitivity of 0.94% and specificity of 0.97% in ocular myasthenia1and is based on the principle that cooler temperatures result in reduced acetylcholinesterase activity.1It involves placing ice on the involved eyelid for at least 2 minutes and comparing the pretest to posttest measurements. The test is considered to have positive results when there is an increase in the size of the palpebral fissure compared with the pretest measurement. This patient had no symptoms of giant cell arteritis, such as headache, scalp tenderness, or jaw claudication, and he was relatively young for this condition, which is why choice A was not the next best option. Neuroimaging would not be the next best step, because his examination findings could not be localized. Computed tomography angiography or magnetic resonance angiography would be indicated in a third nerve palsy, but this patient did not have this, which is why choice B was not correct. He had no orbital signs (eg, proptosis, conjunctival chemosis, eyelid retraction), and an orbital lesion would not explain the ptosis, which is why choice C was not correct. Ocular myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction confined to the ocular muscles. In ocular myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies develop against the acetylcholine receptors (commonly) or other associated proteins at the neuromuscular junction, leading to muscle weakness and fatigability.2Patients typically present with ptosis and diplopia that is worse with muscle use, with normal pupil reactions. While more than 85% of patients with the systemic variant have detectable autoantibodies in their serum, patients with the ocular variant have 45% to 60% sensitivity with the same test.3In seronegative ocular myasthenia gravis, single-fiber electromyography may be used to evaluate neuromuscular transmission.4In this patient, serum acetylcholine receptor antibody tests had negative results, but single-fiber electromyography was highly suggestive of a postsynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder. Initial therapy for ocular myasthenia gravis consists of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, such as 30 to 150 mg of pyridostigmine 3 to 4 times daily.5Many patients need additional immunosuppression for full clinical remission, including prednisone, azathioprine, and mycophenolate mofetil.6Approximately two-thirds of patients with ocular myasthenia gravis will progress to systemic disease,7and patients should be counseled on seeking medical attention if they have clinically significant sequelae, such as difficulty breathing. The patient’s ptosis and diplopia mildly improved with 60 mg of pyridostigmine 3 times daily, and prednisone daily was started at 10 mg and titrated up to 40 mg, resulting in complete remission. At his 6-month follow-up, a slow taper of prednisone was initiated because he continued to have no ptosis and normal ocular motility.

scenario: A 47-year-old man presented with gradual onset of blurry vision in both eyes for several months. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS. Intraocular pressure was 23 mm Hg in both eyes and was more than 21 mm Hg in both eyes on multiple visits. Medical history included hypertension, obesity, left adrenalectomy, and pterygium excision surgery in the left eye. The patient denied previous episodes of blurry vision, history of corticosteroid use, sleep apnea, or type-A personality. Complete review of systems was otherwise negative. Amsler grid testing revealed paracentral metamorphopsia in both eyes. Extraocular motility, pupillary light reactions, and confrontational visual fields were normal. Slitlamp examination and gonioscopy results were normal in both eyes. An external photograph of the patient is shown inFigure 1A. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multiple areas of late pinpoint leakage and patches of mottled hyperfluorescence in both eyes (Figure 1B).

explanation: Bilateral central serous chorioretinopathy secondary to pituitary microadenoma C. Draw morning plasma cortisol levels This patient exhibited signs of hypercortisolism, including central obesity (Figure 1). He had systemic hypertension, which occurs in most patients with endogenous hypercortisolism,1,2and elevated intraocular pressure, which has been reported in endogenous hypercortisolism and can be caused by corticosteroid use.3,4His hemoglobin A1clevel was elevated (6.8%), which is consistent with impaired glucose metabolism in endogenous hypercortisolism.2 Fluorescein angiography showed multiple areas of late pinpoint leakage and guttering, which is patchy, mottled hyperfluorescence caused by gravity-related descending tracts of subretinal fluid (Figure 1). These fluorescein angiography findings are typical of central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC), which is characterized by serous detachment of neurosensory retina/retinal pigment epithelium (Figure 2) and choroidal hyperpermeability. The leakage on fluorescein angiography is most consistent with active CSC, whereas the patches of mottled fluorescence are more typical of chronic CSC. The patient denied corticosteroid exposure; given the possibility of hypercortisolism of unknown cause, he was referred to the endocrinology unit for further evaluation. Cortisol testing (choice C) was performed and showed elevated 8amplasma cortisol (15.2 µg/dL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 27.588). Overnight challenge with 1 mg of dexamethasone resulted in an 8amplasma cortisol of 17.8 µg/dL, confirming hypercortisolism. Adrenocorticotropic hormone levels were not suppressed, raising suspicion for a central cause of hypercortisolism. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling confirmed a central source of adrenocorticotropic hormone, and pituitary magnetic resonance imaging revealed a pituitary microadenoma. The differential diagnosis for this case included CSC associated with exogenous, or rarely, endogenous hypercortisolism, neovascular age-related macular degeneration, polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy or pathologic myopia with choroidal neovascularization, and paraproteinemia. However, the patient’s relatively young age and lack of drusen were not consistent with age-related macular degeneration. Moreover, the patient lacked polypoidal lesions on indocyanine green angiography findings, making polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy less likely. The patient did not have myopia, making pathologic myopia unlikely. Intravitreal injection of an anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agent (choice A) would be an appropriate treatment for CSC with choroidal neovascularization but not in this patient without choroidal neovascularization.5,6Bilateral retinal pigment epithelium detachments can also be found in paraproteinemia, although the patient had normal blood cell counts and did not report any B-signs of malignancy. Therefore, bone marrow biopsy (choice D) was not indicated. Neither oral spironolactone (choice B), a mineralocorticoid antagonist, nor eplerenone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, improve visual acuity in patients with CSC.7,8A workup for underlying causes of hypercortisolism (choice C) should be considered prior to retinal management of CSC in a patient with Cushingoid appearance. Risk factors for CSC include corticosteroid use in any form.9CSC is rarely caused by endogenous hypercortisolism.10Ophthalmologists should be cognizant that while Cushing syndrome is most commonly caused by corticosteroid-containing medications, it may also result from an adrenocorticotropic hormone–secreting pituitary tumor (Cushing disease). The patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary microadenoma. His vision remains stable, but serum cortisol levels have not yet normalized.

scenario: A woman in her 50s with hypertension who was otherwise in good health presented for new ophthalmologic evaluation in the setting of mild, long-standing blurred vision with slight metamorphopsia in the right eye. She had a history of high myopia (approximately 9 diopters [D]OD; 8DOS). Examination revealed an otherwise normal left eye with 20/20 best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA). The right eye demonstrated a BCVA of 20/25 and normal anterior segment, including lenticular examination. Dilated fundus examination showed wrinkling of the neurosensory retina at the fovea (Figure 1A) without posterior vitreous detachment. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography revealed hyperreflective layering on the foveal surface consistent with epiretinal membrane, as well as splitting of the outer plexiform layer with hyporeflective cavities (Figure 1B).

explanation: Foveal retinoschisis with epiretinal membrane in the setting of pathologic myopia D. Observation without considering intervention unless visual acuity deterioration is found A diagnostic explanation for retinal splitting, hyporeflective spaces, or cystoid abnormalities is necessary when evaluating retinal problems with optical coherence tomography, which sometimes can be multifactorial. The differential diagnosis for these findings in the macula includes inherited retinal disorders (eg, X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, Goldmann-Favre syndrome), medications (eg, antimicrotubular agents), vascular insults (eg, retinal vein occlusion), and trauma. In this case, the presence of an epiretinal membrane with pathologic myopia was suggestive of foveoschisis. Visualization can be supplemented by en face images and vitreoretinal interface segmentation. Myopic foveoschisis, typically with associated features, including staphyloma,1can be associated with substantial visual acuity loss that may not always be correctable with surgical intervention. These problems are often compounded by other visual acuity loss from pathologic myopia, such as myopic degeneration in the posterior pole, in addition to epiretinal proliferation or dense remnants of cortical vitreous following posterior vitreous detachment. Foveoschisis does not always have to be accompanied by epiretinal membrane, and the causative mechanism of myopic foveoschisis remains unknown.1 Given mild visual impairment for this patient, observation was elected (choice D) instead of opting for surgical peeling (choice A). Surgery is warranted if there is substantial visual impairment, assessed through BCVA and metamorphopsia by Amsler grid testing. Judgment involves determining the effect on function by considering the patient’s occupation and activities of daily living. It is often reasonable to monitor for clear disease progression before proceeding with vitrectomy and membrane peeling. Many cases are successful with both epiretinal and internal limiting membrane peeling for reducing recurrence.2 Periocular steroids (choice B) may benefit macular edema arising from diabetes or inflammatory conditions, but they are unlikely to be helpful for this causative mechanism of retinoschisis. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition (choice C) with either topical dorzolamide or oral acetazolamide is known to help macular edema associated with retinitis pigmentosa, but it is not typically used for retinoschisis. Spontaneous resolution of foveoschisis without intervention has been reported, independent of the status of the posterior hyaloid.1,3-5Release of epiretinal membrane and posterior hyaloid may follow known age-associated changes at the vitreomacular attachment interface.6Close observation is therefore reasonable in select cases, depending on impairment and overall clinical context. Additional research is needed to further characterize the natural history of this condition, including frequency of progression, spontaneous resolution, and recurrence. Four years after presentation and electing observation, the patient returned with resolution of the foveoschisis and release of posterior hyaloid. She achieved 20/20 OU visual acuity, which was sustained 9 years later (Figure 2).

scenario: A 28-year-old man with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) presented with a recent bilateral and painless decrease of best-corrected visual acuity to light perception OD and counting fingers OS. Results of a slitlamp examination showed iris neovascularization and posterior subcapsular cataract in the right eye and no anterior segment abnormalities, including no iris neovascularization, in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 60 mm Hg in the right eye and 14 mm Hg in the left eye. The fundus in the right eye (Figure, A) showed a total retinal detachment with hemorrhagic prepapillary fibrosis reaching up to the posterior capsule; the left eye (Figure, B) showed peripapillary tractional retinal detachment with proliferative vitreoretinopathy, retinal neovascularization, and vitreous hemorrhage. Fluorescein angiography showed extensive retinal capillary and arteriolar nonperfusion and peripapillary neovascularization in both eyes. The patient denied diabetes, sickle cell disease, radiotherapy exposure, and any ophthalmic history. He was not followed up regularly by an ophthalmologist but had consulted an outside clinic 3 weeks before for a loss of visual acuity, which measured at 20/400 OD and 20/63 OS. Visual acuity preceding this consultation was not known.

explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy–associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy B. Contact the patient’s general practitioner and cardiologist to obtain hemoglobin and cardiac ejection fraction levels Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe X-linked recessive muscular dystrophy caused by absent or altered dystrophin production with an incidence of 1 per 3500 male births.1First symptoms appear around 3 to 5 years of age with most patients requiring the use of a wheelchair by age 12 years. The median survival is 24 to 27 years with major reported causes of death attributable to heart failure and respiratory insufficiency. Duchenne muscular dystrophy–associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy is a rare and rapidly progressive retinal disorder described in patients with DMD, usually after age 20 (range, 18-30) years.2-7Extensive areas of retinal capillary and arteriolar nonperfusion can lead to widespread peripapillary neovascularization. Patients may present late with advanced disease and fronds of neovascular tissue emanating from the optic nerve and iris neovascularization. The pathophysiology of the vasculopathy is not fully understood and is most likely multifactorial. First, the dystrophin is known to be expressed in the retina in the internal limiting membrane and around retinal vessels and is important for neurotransmission because its deficiency produces abnormal transmission between photoreceptors and bipolar cells.8Dystrophin is also expressed on endothelial cells. Nico et al9found alterations in dystrophin-deficient mice affecting the endothelial junctions, vessel permeability, and tissue edema as well as increased expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). The upregulation of VEGF alone is most likely not sufficient to cause vasculopathy and requires other hypoxic or ischemic components.10 Published cases of DMD-associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy usually report respiratory and cardiac insufficiency with a diminished cardiac ejection fraction,2-6which, in conjunction with pathological regulation of endothelial permeability and VEGF in a DMD retina, could potentially induce levels of retinal hypoxia necessary to trigger the massive proliferative retinopathy. One report of DMD-associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy described a patient with normal cardiac function (cardiac ejection fraction of 70%), albeit with respiratory insufficiency, mild anemia, and early diabetes,7that could all have contributed to the proliferative disease. The differential diagnosis includes proliferative diabetic retinopathy and familial exudative vitreoretinopathy. The patient did not have diabetes, and the course of the disease was not typical for familial exudative vitreoretinopathy. According to the patient’s cardiologist, he had a severely altered cardiac ejection fraction of 25%, abnormal lung function with a forced vital capacity of 15%, and anemia with serum hemoglobin levels of 91 g/L (normal range is 140 to 180 g/L; to convert to g/dL, divide by 10). Results of carotid ultrasonography were normal. The chorioretinal biopsy (choice A) would not have been an appropriate way to diagnose and treat the patient, and the anti-VEGF injection (choice C) and panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) alone (choice D) would not have contributed to the repair of the complex retinal detachment. The anti-VEGF agents and PRP should have been used early and aggressively at the first signs of the disease to treat retinal ischemia and prevent neovascularization and rapidly progressing retinal detachment.3,4 The DMD-associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy is an entity rarely seen by ophthalmologists, most likely because most patients with DMD die before the retinopathy develops. With improved survivability, notably due to ventilation therapy, ophthalmologists may see more of these cases in the future. Periodic ophthalmic testing should enable clinicians to detect retinopathy and treat it with PRP and anti-VEGF injections early and with vitrectomy in more advanced cases.4-6 The patient elected to undergo surgery in the left eye, consisting of lensectomy, pars plana vitrectomy, endolaser coagulation, and silicon oil tamponade. The retinal anatomy could not be reestablished because of the extensive retinal fibrosis. The final visual acuity was light perception OD and counting fingers OS, and both eyes remained quiescent and painless.

scenario: A 37-year-old man with no history of vision problems presented with subacute loss of vision in his right eye for 1 week. The patient described a paracentral scotoma that progressed to involve central fixation over the course of 3 days. Two weeks earlier, the patient and his children had developed malaise, low-grade fever, and a rash. He worked in the armed services and denied foreign travel, tick bites, or recent immunization. The patient had been evaluated by his primary care clinician and was referred to an ophthalmologist for further evaluation. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/70 OD and 20/20 OS. Test results of intraocular pressures, ocular motility, and pupillary reactions were normal. Confrontation visual fields showed inferonasal and central defects in the right eye. External examination revealed a macular rash of the scalp and all 4 extremities, including the soles and palms (Figure 1A). Anterior segment examination was normal. Posterior segment examination revealed irregular, gray-white pigmentation of the temporal macula of the right eye without vitritis, optic nerve edema, or vasculitis (Figure 1B). Ocular coherence tomography (OCT) revealed focal, heterogenous disruption of the inner segment ellipsoid zone without neurosensory detachment. Fluorescein angiography showed late staining at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) superotemporal to the fovea. Findings from a dilated fundus examination were normal in the left eye.

explanation: D. Order coxsackievirus serologic testing The subacute development of unilateral vision loss in an otherwise healthy young patient with recent viral illness initially led to a referral for possible optic neuritis. However, the lack of pain or relative afferent pupillary defect and irregular macular pigmentation raised concern for an inflammatory maculopathy, such as acute macular neuroretinopathy or unilateral acute idiopathic maculopathy (UAIM). Although these 2 entities both present with inflammatory changes of the RPE, the unilateral nature and more substantial acuity decline favored UAIM. Furthermore, characteristic unilateral gray-white retinal pigment changes with heterogeneous disruption of the photoreceptor layer and hyperreflective thickening of the apical RPE in the foveal region (Figure 2) on OCT confirmed the diagnosis of UAIM. Despite similarities in temporal profile of vision loss with optic neuritis, UAIM does not involve the retrobulbar optic nerve or intracranial structures, so neuroimaging (choice A) is not indicated. Herpesvirus infection (choice B) may cause focal retinal whitening secondary to acute retinal necrosis but has not been implicated in UAIM. Although hydroxychloroquine and other potential retinal toxins (choice C) can present with similar patterns of maculopathy with ellipsoid zone disruption, they are typically insidious and bilateral. Unilateral acute idiopathic maculopathy is a rare maculopathy first described by Yannuzzi et al1in 1991. Characteristic findings were inflammatory RPE changes with exudative macular detachment and spontaneous near-complete resolution of vision loss over weeks to months following viral illness. A follow-up case series by Freund et al2in 1996 expanded the clinical spectrum of the disease, describing cases with papillitis, bilateral involvement, and fewer retinal hemorrhages. These first series postulated that UAIM is an inflammatory process and noted potential associations with pregnancy, HIV, and coxsackievirus. Coxsackievirus is a well-known cause of the highly contagious hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD) that is characterized by its namesake viral exanthem. In 2004, Beck et al3presented 2 cases of adult-onset HFMD associated with UAIM. The author group posited that coxsackievirus may have been the cause. Subsequently, numerous case reports have been published of patients with UAIM and concomitant adult-onset HFMD,4-8supporting the potential association. Among these reports, there is no consensus regarding treatment, with many clinicians choosing to observe the often self-limited disease. The potential unproven benefit of using systemic corticosteroids that others elected to provide should be balanced with the potential harm for patients at high risk for systemic complications of treatment. Regardless of treatment, the prognosis is generally good, with most patients recovering near-normal vision. The patient was diagnosed with adult-onset HFMD. He elected to receive 60 mg of oral prednisone daily with planned taper over 6 weeks for presumed coxsackievirus-related UAIM. Two weeks later, his uncorrected distance visual acuity improved to 20/20 OD, with subjective reduction in scotoma size. There was substantial reduction of the ellipsoid zone disruption on OCT. After 2 months, the patient’s visual acuity improved to 20/15 OD with near complete resolution of visual field defect and minimal persistent outer retinal changes on OCT.

scenario: A 34-year-old woman presented with photophobia in both eyes. Six months earlier while abroad, the patient had bilateral cosmetic iris implants (BrightOcular) placed. The patient had a mild change in refractive error postoperatively and was offered laser in situ keratomileusis surgery for correction. She did not report any other immediate postoperative complications. For 4 weeks before presentation, she had blurred vision of the right eye. Her visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/25 OS. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 31 mm Hg in the right eye and 17 mm Hg in the left. The pupillary reflex could not be visualized secondary to the iris implants. Slitlamp examination revealed trace anterior chamber cell bilaterally with pigmented keratic precipitates. The implants were overlying the iris structures (Figure 1A). Results of an ultrasonographic biomicroscopy are shown inFigure 1B. Posterior examination was limited by the iris implants, but the optic nerve did not reveal edema or hemorrhages. The peripheral retina could not be visualized in either eye. The patient was prescribed topical prednisolone acetate in both eyes and timolol maleate, dorzolamide hydrochloride, and brimonidine tartrate in the right eye only. On follow-up 2 days later, the IOP in the right eye had decreased to 17 mm Hg.

options.B: Maintain IOP-lowering therapy with continued observation
options.D: Remove the cosmetic iris implants surgically

answer: Remove the cosmetic iris implants surgically
distractors: Maintain IOP-lowering therapy with continued observation
explanation: Uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema syndrome secondary to cosmetic iris implants D. Remove the cosmetic iris implants surgically Herpetic keratouveitis can present with elevated pressure, anterior chamber cells, and keratic precipitates, as in this patient’s case. However, these findings are most commonly unilateral in herpetic disease.1Thus, initiating oral acyclovir (choice C) would not be the most appropriate option. Instead, on the basis of the initial presentation of anterior chamber cells, elevated IOP, and pigmented keratic precipitates, a diagnosis of uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome secondary to the patient’s cosmetic iris implants was made. Initially conceived for use in patients with congenital or traumatic aniridia, iris implants were first used in 1994.2A decade later, anterior chamber iris implants were marketed for cosmetic purposes. These cosmetic implants have been associated with multiple complications aside from UGH syndrome, including corneal decompensation, synechiae formation, iris and retinal neovascularization, and cataracts.3-5 Uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema syndrome was first described in 1978 and traditionally presents when an intraocular chamber lens or haptic rubs against iris tissue, leading to chafing.6However, other sources, such as cosmetic iris implants, have also been reported to be associated with UGH syndrome.5The mechanical irritation of iris tissue may lead to the triad of uveitis, elevated IOP, and hyphema, although the diagnosis is often made without the complete triad. Diagnosis of UGH syndrome is clinical but can be aided by imaging. Ultrasonographic biomicroscopy can be used to visualize the position of intraocular lenses or other iatrogenic sources of iris irritation. Optical coherence tomography can be used to diagnose and monitor cystoid macular edema. The definitive treatment in UGH syndrome is removal of the inciting cause of iris irritation.7Topical IOP-lowering therapy (choice B) could be used as a temporary measure but would not be definitive therapy. Although IOP-lowering therapy could be used as a bridge to implant removal, it would not address the inciting factor, irritation of the iris by the implants. Additionally, IOP-lowering drops would not prevent other complications, including uveitis, ocular ischemia, and corneal decompensation. Surgery to place a glaucoma implant device (choice A) would not be an appropriate first step because though it may lower the IOP, it would not address the underlying cause of mechanical iris irritation. In addition, the patient’s pressure was controlled with topical therapy; incisional glaucoma surgery for IOP control would be premature at this juncture. Instead, the definitive treatment in this case is removal of the inciting factor (choice D), the cosmetic iris implants. In this case, despite counseling, the patient refused to have the implants removed. She was lost to follow-up for 4 months. On her return, the patient’s visual acuity had deteriorated to 20/400 OD and hand motions OS. The IOP was elevated to 33 mm Hg OD and 38 mm Hg OS. Diffuse keratic precipitates and 2+ anterior chamber cells were seen in both eyes. Both optic nerves showed considerable advanced cupping compared with the initial visit, and robust fine radial neovascularization at the optic nerve head was visualized in the left eye (Figure 2). At this time, the patient agreed to surgery, and both implants were removed.

scenario: A 26-year-old man presented with reduced visual acuity in both eyes since early childhood. He had short stature (1.52 m [−3.6 SD]) and progeroid appearance. His parents and brother had normal stature. His medical history was significant for frequent upper respiratory tract infections since infancy. He had no intellectual disability, neurologic symptoms, or hearing impairment. There was no family history of visual impairment or neurologic disorders. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/50 OS. Intraocular pressure was normal. He could not identify any Ishihara color plate. Slitlamp examination was unremarkable. Dilated fundus examination results showed diffuse optic atrophy (OA) and fine pigmentary mottling changes at the fovea in both eyes (Figure 1A). Electroretinography (ERG) showed normal dark-adapted responses and severely reduced light-adapted responses. Optical coherence tomography showed thinning of retinal nerve fiber layers and disruption of outer nuclear layers and the ellipsoid zone at the center of the fovea (Figure 1B). explanation: Short stature, OA, Pelger-Huët anomaly syndrome Diagnosis of hereditary OA is challenging for ophthalmologists, especially when combined with retinal dystrophy. Because the optic nerve may have variable degrees of temporal pallor in cone dystrophy, cone disorders should be included in the differential diagnosis. Optic atrophy is usually accompanied byCACNA1Fcongenital stationary night blindness,1or it can be a late manifestation of retinitis pigmentosa. However, patients with congenital stationary night blindness typically have normal fundus and negative ERGs in scotopic response. Spinocerebellar ataxia andSSBP1variant also cause OA and variable retinal degeneration.2,3 Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed and revealed novel compound heterozygousNBASc.3493del:p.(Val1165Serfs*31) c.5740C>T:p.(Arg1914Cys) variants. The 2 variants were in-trans, confirmed by trio WES, and are likely pathogenic.4Results of further workups, including peripheral blood smear examination, showed bilobulated granulocytes (Figure 2) and hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG, 524.4 mg/dL [normal range, 800-1800 mg/dL]; IgA, 19.0 mg/dL [normal range, 105-500 mg/dL]; to convert IgG and IgA to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10); however, liver enzyme levels were normal. TheNBASgene encodes a component protein of the syntaxin 18 complex and is involved in Golgi-to-endoplasmic reticulum transport.5﻿NBASgene mutations cause either infantile liver failure syndrome (OMIM616483) or short stature, OA, Pelger-Huët anomaly (SOPH) syndrome (OMIM614800) depending on the location of the variants.6TheNBASgene has 3 functional domains as follows: beta-propeller domain and Sec39 domain, plus an unknown function of the C-terminal. The novel C-terminal variant discovered in the patient is the same amino acid residue p.(Arg1914His) known to be a founder mutation in the Yakut population.7To our knowledge, hepatic dysfunction has never been reported in patients carrying the homozygous p.(Arg1914His) variant,7but variable hepatic involvements have been observed in patients with compound heterozygousNBASvariants.8A SOPH syndrome diagnosis is based on the clinical constellation of short stature, senile facial appearance, OA, Pelger-Huët anomaly, and normal intelligence. The key feature in this case is the extreme short stature, progeroid appearance, and cone dystrophy. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (choice A) was deferred because the patient had no neurologic signs or symptoms. Wolfram syndrome should be considered in the differential diagnosis. Although growth hormone deficiency has been reported in Wolfram syndrome, checking the blood glucose and hemoglobin A1clevels (choice B) are inappropriate given the absence of diabetes and hearing impairment at his age.9Moreover, visual acuity in Wolfram syndrome is typically worse then 20/200. Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 also causes variable degrees of cone dystrophy and OA,3but trinucleotide repeat sequencing (choice C) was deferred because the patient had no ataxia. Therefore, WES is the most appropriate next step. The ophthalmologic manifestation of SOPH syndrome is characterized by OA and color vision loss. Other ophthalmologic manifestations, including horizontal nystagmus, retinal dystrophy, foveal hypoplasia, gray sclera, and corneal opacity, were also reported.7,8,10Vision loss and OA can be initial manifestations in SOPH syndrome. Recognition of syndromic features and a high index of suspicion can identify the underlying causes of OA. In addition, theNBASgene should be included in the targeted workup for both OA and cone dystrophy. During the 5 years of follow-up, the patient’s visual acuity was maintained. We advised regular monitoring of liver function.

scenario: A 65-year-old man presented with worsening right eye pain and purulent discharge. He reported being hit in the face by a tree branch several days prior. His medical history was notable for HIV, with a last known CD4 lymphocyte count of 112 cells/mm3and variable adherence to antiretroviral therapy. At an outside hospital, cultures were obtained, and treatment was initiated with ofloxacin eye drops, 0.3%, ciprofloxacin hydrochloride ointment, 0.3%, and oral moxifloxacin hydrochloride, 400 mg daily. His symptoms worsened, and he was referred 3 days later for further evaluation. On examination, visual acuity in the right eye was hand motions. The left eye examination results were unremarkable. Slitlamp examination was limited by patient discomfort but revealed purulent discharge, a markedly inflamed conjunctiva, diffuse cornea opacification and thinning, and a flat anterior chamber. Given the history of tree branch trauma, the patient was brought to the operating room. Intraoperatively, a 0.5-mm corneal perforation was identified within an area of thinning (Figure, A). Microbial cultures were repeated, and corneal glue was applied. Gram stain of the purulent discharge demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes only. All subsequent microbiology cultures were negative. Despite treatment with topical fortified vancomycin, 25 mg/mL, tobramycin, 13.3 mg/mL, intravenous levofloxacin, 750 mg daily, and doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily, the purulent conjunctivitis and corneal stromal necrosis did not improve (Figure, B).

options.A: Obtain initial culture results from the referring physician
options.B: Pursue serologic workup for autoimmune disease
options.D: Return to the operating room for therapeutic keratoplasty

answer: Obtain initial culture results from the referring physician
distractors: Pursue serologic workup for autoimmune disease
Return to the operating room for therapeutic keratoplasty
explanation: A. Obtain initial culture results from the referring physician Given persistent marked purulence and stromal necrosis, the negative culture results were surprising. However, these microbiology studies were obtained while the patient was receiving broad-spectrum topical antibiotic therapy. Initial culture results were obtained from the referring physician (choice A), which grewNeisseria gonorrhoeae. The patient then disclosed that his partner recently had a penile ulcer. He was immediately treated with saline lavages and single doses of intramuscular ceftriaxone sodium, 1 g, and oral azithromycin, 1 g, for gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis. Although this patient was initially transferred with concern for a traumatic ruptured globe, the history of prior tree trauma was a red herring. The persistent purulence and corneal stromal necrosis raised concern for infection. Yield of ocular surface cultures are decreased when samples are obtained with concurrent topical antimicrobial therapy.1This case also emphasizes the potential importance of follow-up on primary data. When patients are transferred between institutions with different medical record systems, information can be lost. Serologic workup for autoimmune keratitis (choice B) is not the preferred answer because the hyperpurulence and beefy conjunctival injection would be atypical for this sterile inflammatory presentation. Starting empirical treatment for acanthamoeba (choice C) is incorrect because hyperpurulence is unusual in acanthamoeba keratitis, and the patient had no freshwater risk factors or history of contact lens wear. With progressive corneal necrosis, returning to the operating room for therapeutic keratoplasty (choice D) may have been required; however, the initial best step in management is to obtain confirmative diagnosis. Gonorrheal keratoconjunctivitis is due to infection withN gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus. In populations other than neonates, transmission mostly occurs via direct sexual contact with infective secretions or indirectly via fomite transmission.2A study in Ireland found the prevalence of gonococcal conjunctivitis to be 0.19 cases per 1000 patients evaluated for eye emergencies, with the majority in young adult males.3 Treatment of gonorrheal keratoconjunctivitis is both systemic and local. Recommended systemic treatment includes administration of intramuscular ceftriaxone, 1 g, in a single dose.4,5Systemic azithromycin, 1 g, in a single dose or oral doxycycline, 100 mg twice a day for 7 days, is also added owing to frequent coinfection withChlamydia trachomatis.6Topical treatment is ancillary and can include a fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and/or saline lavages.3,7Gonorrhea is a reportable disease. Notification of risk of this disease and treatment of all sexual partners is necessary. Gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis may lead to serious ocular complications. Corneal stromal necrosis can occur, as with this case, in a fulminant fashion. Treatment of corneal stromal necrosis depends on the size and extent of stromal involvement and whether perforation of the cornea is present. Medical management of corneal stromal necrosis includes systemic antigonorrheal antibiotic therapy and anticollagenase medications. Surgical management for descemetoceles and perforations may include glue, amniotic membrane transplant, therapeutic lamellar, or full-thickness corneal and conjunctival flaps. In this case, corneal gluing was pursued because the area of perforation was small. The diagnosis of gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis should be considered in individuals who present with markedly purulent conjunctivitis with or without genital symptoms. History may not be forthcoming. Presentation classically includes conjunctival injection, eyelid edema, hyperpurulent discharge, and preauricular lymphadenopathy. With prompt, effective treatment, the infection can be eradicated and complications, such as corneal melt and perforation, can be avoided. After treatment with intramuscular ceftriaxone, 1 g, oral azithromycin, 1 g, gentle saline lavage, and topical moxifloxacin, 0.5% four times a day, this patient’s anterior chamber reformed, the corneal epithelial defect decreased in size, and iris structures were visible owing to improvement in the corneal infiltrate. The patient was subsequently discharged from the hospital and lost to follow-up thereafter.

caption: A, Optical coherence tomography (OCT) image shows schisis of the outer plexiform layer in the foveal and parafoveal regions (white arrowhead) and schisis of the inner retina in the temporal macula (yellow arrowhead). B, An OCT image shows schisis of the outer plexiform layer in the foveal and parafoveal regions (arrowhead).
scenario: A 64-year-old woman in excellent general health who was not taking any medications was referred for evaluation of an epiretinal membrane of her right eye. She reported no blurry vision, metamorphopsia, photopsias, floaters, or nyctalopia, and she had no history of refractive surgical procedures, ocular surgical procedures, or trauma. Her family history was negative for ocular conditions, and there was no consanguinity in her family. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU with correction (plano +0.25 × 153 OD and −0.50 + 0.25 × 009 OS). External and anterior segment examination results were unremarkable except for mild nuclear sclerotic cataracts. Results of a dilated ophthalmoscopic examination showed radial spokelike striae of the fovea, with a central cyst in the right eye and macular edema of the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging of the right macula showed cystlike changes in the outer retina in the foveal and parafoveal regions and in the inner retina in the temporal macula. Optical coherence tomography imaging of the left macula showed cystlike changes in the outer retina in the inferior macula (Figure). Of note, OCT scans of the optic nerves did not reveal an optic disc pit.

options.C: Prescribe antivascular endothelial growth factor therapy
options.D: Prescribe topical prednisolone or ketorolac therapy

distractors: Prescribe antivascular endothelial growth factor therapy
Prescribe topical prednisolone or ketorolac therapy
explanation: Stellate nonhereditary idiopathic foveomacular retinoschisis We present a case of a 64-year-old woman with no ocular history and a negative family history. The OCT imaging showed schisis primarily of the outer retina that was consistent with bilateral stellate foveomacular retinoschisis. The most appropriate next step is to order an electroretinogram (ERG) (choice A) to rule out congenital juvenile X-linked retinoschisis (CXLR), which is caused by a variation in theRS1gene (OMIM300839). Congenital juvenile X-linked retinoschisis typically has an electronegative ERG but can be variable and even normal in some patients. Congenital juvenile X-linked retinoschisis is most commonly found in males; however, there are reports of females with this disease due to lyonization or homozygosity.1,2This patient was unlikely to be a carrier because she did not have white flecks in the periphery on fundus examination and had a negative family history. The patient’s ERG was unremarkable in both eyes. Performing pars plana vitrectomy (choice B) and prescribing antivascular endothelial growth factor therapy (choice C) would not be the preferred answer because they are not proven to benefit patients with stellate nonhereditary idiopathic foveomacular retinoschisis (SNIFR). Both are inappropriate as the next step in management of this patient. Prescribing topical prednisolone or ketorolac therapy (choice D) was not indicated because the cystic areas were from retinoschisis and not cystoid macular edema. Foveomacular retinoschisis can be associated with optic pit maculopathy, myopic retinoschisis, retinitis pigmentosa, glaucoma, vitreomacular traction, or degenerative retinoschisis, which were ruled out by the patient’s clinical examination results, ERG, and imaging. Enhanced S-cone syndrome is inconsistent with the patient’s good vision throughout her life and the unremarkable fundus examination and ERG results. There are no known genetic associations with SNIFR. However, testing to rule out other genetic diseases, such as retinitis pigmentosa or X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, which can be associated with a similar appearance, could be performed as indicated based on clinical history and findings. The patient was not taking any medications associated with retinoschisis, including niacin or taxanes. The patient was asymptomatic, had excellent visual acuity, and had no evidence of hereditary or acquired retinoschisis. Given this clinical picture, the patient likely had bilateral SNIFR. A case of bilateral non–X-linked macular schisis was described inGass’ Atlas of Macular Diseases3and possibly represented a case of SNIFR. In the largest reported case series, most patients were asymptomatic or had minimal symptoms with unilateral findings.4In addition, splitting was most common in the outer plexiform layer, with lesser involvement of the outer nuclear layer, as was seen in this patient.4The typical stellate pattern of the macula was visible in 1 eye of this patient, but reports have been published of patients with SNIFR without this fundus finding, perhaps due to concurrent neovascular age-related macular degeneration.5 SNIFR is typically managed with observation, as patients generally have good vision.6Treatment of SNIFR with dorzolamide therapy has been reported to result in complete resolution of SNIFR and improvement in vision.7We could consider this option if the patient’s vision deteriorated. Performing surgical procedures is not indicated for these patients. It is important to consider SNIFR in a patient with foveomacular retinoschisis without a family history, degenerative condition, or acquired etiology. Follow-up was indicated to monitor for possible loss of visual acuity. There are no clear guidelines on frequency of follow-up. One study reports biannual follow-up of a patient with unilateral SNIFR and best-corrected visual acuity of 20/20 in the involved eye.6 This patient was followed up every 6 months. If the patient becomes symptomatic or shows progression of disease on OCT imaging, the patient should be more closely monitored with shorter intervals for follow-up.

caption: A slitlamp photograph of the right eye shows a translucent grayish-white cystic mass in the inferonasal aspect of the iris stroma.
scenario: A 14-month-old boy presented with a sudden-onset, rapidly enlarging lesion in the right eye detected by his parents 2 weeks earlier. The patient had normal tracking bilaterally. Under anesthesia, findings from an examination of the right eye revealed an inferonasal translucent gray-white iris mass with numerous intralesional lacy cystic structures (Figure 1). There was no microphthalmia, cataract, lens subluxation, anterior or posterior synechiae, glaucoma, or uveitis. Findings from a fundus examination were normal. High-resolution anterior segment echography results revealed an iridociliary mass that extended posteriorly to the pars plicata with overall dimensions of 7.7 × 6.0 × 1.9 mm. There were no associated calcifications, retrolental membranes, or seeding.
explanation: The differential diagnosis of an amelanotic iris mass in a young child includes retinoblastoma, medulloepithelioma, juvenile xanthogranuloma, leukemia, and metastatic cancer. In this patient, the absence of intralesional calcifications or retinal tumors would be atypical for retinoblastoma. The absence of characteristic skin lesions and a yellowish-orange, vascularized iris mass is unusual for juvenile xanthogranuloma. Leukemia and metastatic cancer are unlikely in an otherwise healthy young child. The translucent tumor with intralesional cystic structures is characteristic of medulloepithelioma. Medulloepithelioma is a rare tumor that was first described in 1892 and has also been referred to ascarcinoma primitif,terato-neuroma, anddiktyoma.1,2Although retinoblastoma and medulloepithelioma both arise from primitive neuroepithelium derived from the inner layer of the optic cup,3their clinical features are distinct. Retinoblastomas are white vascularized retinal tumors that usually arise before 2 years of age. They frequently contain intratumoral calcifications and are multifocal and bilateral in patients with germlineRB1(OMIM180200) variants.4In contrast, medulloepitheliomas arise from the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium and most commonly present as a grayish-white translucent mass involving the ciliary body and/or iris.1Characteristic features of medulloepithelioma include multiple intralesional cysts and a neoplastic retrolenticular membrane. Because of the ciliary body origin and slow growth of medulloepithelioma, diagnosis is often delayed until an older age (median age of 5 years) than in retinoblastoma.5Presenting symptoms and signs include decreased vision, ocular pain, cataract, and glaucoma. Ultrasound biomicroscopy may help identify a retroiridal ciliary body tumor. Histopathologically, medulloepithelioma demonstrates pseudostratified loops of embryonic neuroglial structures with a surrounding matrix of hyaluronase-rich mesenchymal tissue.1Medulloepithelioma can be classified as nonteratoid or teratoid, the former resembling ciliary epithelium and the latter displaying differentiation of multiple cell lineages.1 Although most cases of intraocular medulloepithelioma are sporadic, 5% of cases are associated with a hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome attributed to germline variants in theDICER1gene (OMIM606241) and associated with pleuropulmonary blastoma.5In addition, 20% of cases are associated with persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous.6 The diagnosis of an iridociliary medulloepithelioma was made on the basis of the clinical characteristics of the iris mass. Because of its malignant potential, observation is not recommended (choice A). Biopsy is generally not performed because of concern for dissemination of malignant cells (choice B). Enucleation is the preferred treatment in large invasive tumors, owing to the high recurrence rate after local surgical resection. Plaque radiotherapy is a reasonable globe-sparing therapy in localized tumors that can be adequately covered by the plaque (choice C).2Although intra-arterial chemotherapy is an established treatment option for retinoblastoma, there are no data to support its use for medulloepithelioma (choice D). In this patient, findings from a baseline systemic evaluation were negative for pleuropulmonary blastoma or metastatic disease. The patient underwent treatment with iodine 125 plaque brachytherapy, with a total dose of 40 Gy directed to the tumor apex. There was complete regression within 4 weeks following brachytherapy (Figure 2) and no local recurrence or metastasis after 6 years of follow-up. Final best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OD.

caption: Fluorescein angiographic photograph at presentation showing mild leakage of retinal vasculature and retinal pigmented epithelium changes at the posterior pole in both eyes (A and B) along with vitreous opacities in the left eye (B).
scenario: A 65-year-old woman was referred for symptoms of painless and progressive bilateral loss of central and peripheral vision over the last 6 months, associated with floaters in the left eye. The patient reported difficulty in performing essential daily tasks, such as driving and walking without assistance. She denied photopsias. Her previous ocular and medical history were unremarkable. She denied any systemic symptoms as well as any family history of inherited ocular diseases. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/32 OU. Fundus examination results showed attenuated arterial and venous retinal vessels and slight retinal pigmented epithelium changes at the posterior pole, consisting of atrophy and pigment migration in both eyes, associated with vitreous opacities in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography examination results showed a mild leakage of arterial and venous retinal vasculature (Figure). Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography exhibited disruption at the photoreceptor level and multifocal hyperreflective material depositions at the retinal pigmented epithelium level. Computerized perimetry demonstrated severe visual field bilateral constriction. Full-field electroretinography showed decreased scotopic and photopic responses. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable, and an extensive workup for underlying infectious or inflammatory causes was unrevealing.

options.A: Obtain a temporal artery biopsy specimen owing to suspicion of Horton disease
options.B: Perform molecular analysis for heritable retinal degeneration
options.C: Investigate serum positivity for antiretinal antibodies and obtain an extensive workup to rule out a malignant neoplasm
options.D: Obtain a diagnostic pars plana vitrectomy with vitreous and aqueous sampling for cytologic analysis

answer: Investigate serum positivity for antiretinal antibodies and obtain an extensive workup to rule out a malignant neoplasm
distractors: Obtain a temporal artery biopsy specimen owing to suspicion of Horton disease
Perform molecular analysis for heritable retinal degeneration
Obtain a diagnostic pars plana vitrectomy with vitreous and aqueous sampling for cytologic analysis
explanation: C. Investigate serum positivity for antiretinal antibodies and obtain an extensive workup to rule out a malignant neoplasm Autoimmune retinopathy (AIR) is a rare form of immune-mediated retinal degeneration. It is characterized by progressive vision loss along with electroretinographic, visual field abnormalities, and the presence of circulating ARAs. Autoimmune retinopathy can be categorized as paraneoplastic (pAIR), which includes cancer-associated retinopathy and melanoma-associated retinopathy, or nonparaneoplastic in the absence of a malignant neoplasm.1,2 Diagnosis remains a challenge because of its variable presentation and fundus appearance, which may be initially normal or with minimal unrevealing alterations despite central vision loss and a severely decreased visual field.1,2Moreover, in contrast with previous reported cases,3,4the patient did not show any systemic symptoms that would have been helpful toward the diagnosis. A differential diagnosis might include heritable retinal degenerations, because clinical findings in AIR, including peripheral visual field loss, reduced electroretinogram waveforms, retinal pigmented epithelium atrophic changes, pigment migration, and photoreceptor loss on optical coherence tomography, can be suggestive of heritable diseases, such as retinitis pigmentosa.5In this case, molecular analysis for heritable retinal degenerations (choice B) would not have been the preferred next step because the patient had no family history of inherited ocular diseases and did not experience typical symptoms, such as nyctalopia, photophobia, or dyschromatopsia. Furthermore, the relatively rapid progression of photoreceptor loss was not typical for retinitis pigmentosa and no bone spicule-like pigmentary changes were present during the fundus examination. The presence of circulating ARAs is important in the pathophysiology and diagnosis of AIR, although it is not pathognomonic, as they have been identified in other retinal diseases, such as uveitis,6in patients with systemic autoimmune disorders,7and in healthy controls.8Given the absence of standardized diagnostic criteria, it has been proposed that an AIR diagnosis should require serum positivity for ARAs associated with progressive loss of visual acuity, visual field defects, and abnormal responses on electroretinography, in the absence of fundus lesions or degenerative retinal disease that might explain these pathologic findings.1,2 Therefore, given the clinical features found in the patient, investigating the presence of ARAs (choice C) was considered to be the most suitable next step to confirm the diagnostic suspicion of AIR. Furthermore, because serum positivity for ARAs and visual symptoms may be present many years before detecting malignant neoplasms in patients with pAIR,9,10an oncologic workup was deemed appropriate for clarifying the paraneoplastic nature of the AIR. Obtaining a diagnostic pars plana vitrectomy with vitreous and aqueous sampling for cytologic analysis (choice D) would not have provided useful information for definitively clarifying the diagnosis and would not have guided us toward the detection of malignant neoplasms. Obtaining a temporal artery biopsy specimen because of suspicion of Horton disease (choice A) would not have been the proper management option. In fact, the patient did not experience typical symptoms, such as headache, jaw claudication, sensitivity on the scalp, or prominent temporal arteries. The patient underwent antiretinal antibody testing that demonstrated reactivity to multiple ARAs. She was referred to the oncology department to undergo a systemic workup for malignant neoplasms and was found to be affected by stage IV, poorly differentiated, gastric adenocarcinoma with multiple metastasis to the abdominal and supraclavicular lymph nodes. She started palliative chemotherapy with FLOT regimen (5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, and docetaxel). After 4 months, the treatment helped to slow the progression of visual field loss, with preservation of central vision and best-corrected visual acuity improvement to 20/25 OU. In addition, a regression of the vitreous opacities in the left eye was detected.

caption: Fundus image shows inferior retinal whitening with a round, discrete white infiltrate overlying the optic nerve. The arrowheads point to sparing in the distribution of the cilioretinal artery. Inset, Intravenous fluorescein angiography shows an inferior filling defect consistent with a hemicentral retinal artery occlusion.
scenario: A 55-year-old man was referred to the eye clinic for unilateral uveitis and 2 days of sudden vision loss in his right eye. He reported experiencing light sensitivity and mild eye pain. He was in otherwise good health without any chronic medical problems. He reported receiving anticoagulation therapy in the past for a mitral valve problem. His visual acuity was 20/200 OD and 20/20 OS. The examination of the left eye was unremarkable. Slitlamp examination of his right eye revealed 3+ anterior chamber inflammation with vitreous cells. An examination of the dilated fundus showed optic nerve edema with an overlying white infiltrate. In addition, there was inferior retinal whitening consistent with an artery occlusion (Figure 1A). The whitening was attributable to inner retina ischemia, with sparing in the distribution of the cilioretinal artery. An inferior hemicentral retinal artery occlusion was confirmed on intravenous fluorescein angiography (Figure 1B). No embolus was noted at any retinal artery branch points. Notably, a dog bit the patient’s hand 2 months before presentation. Since that time, the patient developed a persistent cough, night sweats, and low-grade fevers that were treated unsuccessfully with 2 courses of oral antibiotics.

options.A: Prescribe a course of oral prednisone
options.B: Perform audiometry evaluation for hearing loss with Susac syndrome
options.C: Obtain blood cultures and an echocardiogram
options.D: Evaluate carotid arteries as a potential embolic source

answer: Obtain blood cultures and an echocardiogram
distractors: Prescribe a course of oral prednisone
Perform audiometry evaluation for hearing loss with Susac syndrome
Evaluate carotid arteries as a potential embolic source
explanation: Hemicentral retinal artery occlusion secondary to septic embolus C. Obtain blood cultures and an echocardiogram This patient experienced a hemicentral retinal artery occlusion with early endogenous endophthalmitis secondary to a septic embolus in the setting of bacterial endocarditis with bacteremia fromStreptococcus viridans. This retinal artery occlusion was presumptively related to the recent dog bite and an underlying diagnosis of mitral valve prolapse. Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis is an uncommon subset of endophthalmitis, accounting for approximately 2% to 8% of all endophthalmitis cases.1A systematic review of endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis showed that most patients (77%) had an identifiable preexisting condition, 64% had an identifiable extraocular focus of infection, and 8% had endocarditis.2As in this patient, 73% of patients in the review had systemic symptoms preceding ocular symptoms.2Despite adequate treatment, visual prognosis remains poor for most patients with endogenous endophthalmitis.3 In addition to the unifying diagnosis discussed above, the differential diagnosis at initial presentation included both noninfectious uveitis and classic causes of retinal artery occlusions. Although rare, there have been reports of artery occlusion in the setting of uveitic conditions, such as Behçet disease.4However, an initial course of oral prednisone (choice A) is inappropriate when infectious causes have not been ruled out, especially given the persistent fevers. Susac syndrome presents with multiple recurrent branch retinal artery occlusions that are not at branch points, along with leakage at occlusion sites. This patient’s clinical picture was not consistent with Susac syndrome; thus, audiometry (choice B) would not have been warranted. The correct answer is obtaining blood cultures and an echocardiogram given the history of previous valve disease (choice C). Obtaining a carotid ultrasound to identify embolic sources (choice D) is always prudent in patients presenting with retinal artery occlusions given the high risk of critical neurologic disease.5Concomitant uveitis and a white vitreous infiltrate pointed to an infectious source, making a carotid workup secondary. This case highlights the importance of noting medical history and systemic symptoms when encountering an atypical presentation of a classic ocular condition. Ignoring the systemic symptoms could have led to missing a life-threatening diagnosis. With the patient’s underlying heart condition, weeks of systemic symptoms following a dog bite, and the ophthalmic findings, the clinical suspicion for systemic infection was high. This patient had a life-threatening illness requiring immediate treatment with other specialists. Ophthalmologists must maintain a high index of suspicion for serious extraocular conditions and continue to think beyond the eye when evaluating a patient’s clinical picture. This patient was sent immediately to the emergency department for a full infectious workup and echocardiogram. Blood cultures grewS viridans, and the infectious disease service recommended intravenous ceftriaxone. Transesophageal echocardiogram showed mitral valve prolapse with a 9-mm mitral valve vegetation as the likely source of the septic embolus (Figure 2). An adjuvant injection of intravitreal vancomycin was administered because of worsening vitritis. On follow-up, inflammation had resolved; however, vision loss persisted secondary to the artery occlusion.

caption: Slitlamp photograph of the left eye after subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide injection shows 2 temporal nodules (asterisks), conjunctival hyperemia, and surrounding scleral thinning (yellow arrowheads). Superiorly, remnant subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide can be seen (white arrowhead).
scenario: A 50-year-old woman presented with left eye redness and headaches for 2 months. Results from a previous computed tomographic scan of the head were unremarkable. She denied ocular disease, trauma, or surgery. She had no medical problems aside from chronic back pain due to a herniated disc. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/25 OS. Intraocular pressure, extraocular motility, and pupillary examination results were normal. The right eye was unremarkable. Examination of the left eye showed 2 temporal scleral nodules with surrounding hyperemia and no scleromalacia. She experienced substantial pain with palpation. Posterior examination results were unremarkable. The results of the following laboratory tests were all unremarkable: tuberculosis interferon-γ release assay, rapid plasma reagin, fluorescent treponemal antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and angiotensin-converting enzyme. The rheumatoid factor level (18 IU/mL [normal range, <14 IU/mL]) and C-reactive protein level (26 mg/L [normal range, 0-5 mg/L]) were elevated. In addition, Lyme IgG, IgM, and reflex Western blot assays were positive for antibodies. The patient denied travel to Lyme-endemic regions, tick bites, or rashes. The patient started oral prednisone therapy for possible rheumatoid arthritis (RA)–associated nodular scleritis, doxycycline therapy for positive Lyme studies, and was referred to a rheumatologist for further RA evaluation. Two weeks after presentation and initiation of oral prednisone therapy, the patient noted improvement in pain, but the scleral nodules and hyperemia persisted. Therefore, subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide (0.5 mL of 40 mg/mL) was administered to the left eye. Further confirmatory RA workup by rheumatology did not reveal other systemic findings thought to be associated with RA on review of symptoms or clinical examination. The patient's back pain was associated with her herniated disc. Subsequently, the patient’s examination results showed new scleral thinning of the left eye with persistence of the scleral nodules (Figure 1).

options.C: Transition to noncorticosteroid systemic immunosuppressive therapy

distractors: Transition to noncorticosteroid systemic immunosuppressive therapy
explanation: B. Perform a scleral biopsy Anterior scleritis, the most common form of scleritis, presents with eye redness, substantial pain, and globe tenderness.1Many systemic diseases are associated with scleritis, and diagnosing underlying systemic conditions is important in managing ocular disease. Etiologies include autoimmune, infectious, and traumatic causes. Of autoimmune causes, RA is the most common.2 Treatment options for autoimmune scleritis include oral prednisone and noncorticosteroid systemic immunosuppressive therapies. However, increasing the oral prednisone dosage (choice A) or starting noncorticosteroid systemic immunosuppressive therapy (choice C) would not be the best course of action in this clinical context. The cause of scleritis was still unknown. Immunosuppression in the setting of an infectious origin could worsen the disease. Although she had a mildly elevated rheumatoid factor level, results of further testing by a rheumatologist did not support a diagnosis of RA-associated scleritis. Lyme disease can present with ocular inflammation, including scleritis, but not with rapid scleral thinning or suppuration.3,4There was also no travel to endemic areas, rash, or tick bites, or improvement with doxycycline therapy. Repeating doxycycline treatment (choice D) would therefore not be the most appropriate selection. Of note, although the scleritis initially improved symptomatically with oral prednisone therapy, it worsened with new necrosis after subconjunctival triamcinolone injection, raising concern for a nonspirochetal infection. Performing a scleral biopsy and culture (choice B) was the most direct way to evaluate the patient at this point. Local triamcinolone injection can be a useful adjunctive therapy in nonnecrotizing anterior scleritis but should be avoided in cases with necrosis owing to the risk of scleral melt and perforation.5In scleritis of unknown etiology without initial necrosis, as in this case, local corticosteroid injection should be cautiously administered with close observation, and a biopsy should be performed if indicated. A scleral biopsy was performed in the operating room under local anesthesia. Dissection of the scleral nodules released purulent material, which was cultured. Necrotic sclera was debrided, and an amniotic membrane was sutured over the scleral thinning. Cultures from surgery grewMycobacterium abscessus1 week later. The patient then started treatment with topical amikacin sulfate eyedrops (8 mg/mL every hour) and oral clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily), and was given a 1-mL subconjunctival injection of amikacin sulfate (40 mg/mL). Infection, most commonly bacteria, causes 5% to 10% of scleritis cases.6,7Ocular surgery or trauma are predisposing factors especially in rare, nontuberculous mycobacterial infections, which overwhelmingly occur after surgery or trauma.8Obtaining a good clinical history is therefore essential. The patient had no prior ocular trauma or surgical procedures performed. An infectious cause was suspected owing to worsening of her condition subsequent to local injection of depot corticosteroids, prompting performance of a biopsy. Paradoxical worsening or failure of scleritis to improve with corticosteroid therapy should suggest an infection. Debridement during the biopsy was an important adjunct to medical treatment. During 6 weeks of treatment with topical amikacin and oral clarithromycin, the patient reported resolution of pain. The hyperemia improved, and the scleral thinning stabilized (Figure 2). Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 + 2 OS 3 months after surgery. Salvage of this eye was possible because a biopsy was performed early, facilitating control of the infection with topical, injectable, and oral antibiotic therapies.

caption: Preoperative photograph shows orthotropic eye position during a period of inattention. Note the right esotropia and right dissociated vertical divergence during left eye fixation at near (left inset) and larger left esotropia during right eye fixation at near (right inset).
scenario: A 33-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of intermittent esotropia. When playing video games at a distance or when reading, she developed oscillopsia with eyestrain and noted that her right eye turned up and in. She had undergone strabismus surgery for crossed eyes as a young child and more recently had laser in situ keratomileusis performed. She was medically healthy and neurodevelopmentally normal but had been born 4½ weeks premature. There was no family history of strabismus, and she denied diplopia. On examination, corrected visual acuity was 20/30 − 2 OD and 20/15 OS. Both pupils reacted briskly to light with no afferent pupillary defect. She had 1+ apparent overaction of the right inferior oblique and superior rectus muscles. When she was inattentive, her eyes appeared to be straight (Figure 1). Prism and alternate cover testing during near fixation showed a right esotropia and dissociated vertical divergence when fixing with her preferred left eye (Figure 1, left inset) and a larger left esotropia during forced fixation with her right eye (Figure 1, right inset). She had no cycloplegic refractive error, and retinal examination showed no objective torsion. Placement of +3.00 lenses eliminated her esotropia at near but could not be used to alleviate her symptoms at distance, showing a high accommodation-to-convergence ratio.
explanation: The termdissociated horizontal deviation(DHD) was originally used to describe a unique form of intermittent exotropia in which the measured exodeviation was larger with 1 eye fixating than the other.1-4In some cases, the exodeviation resolves or converts to a large esodeviation when the patient fixates with the nonpreferred eye. Associated clinical findings include latent nystagmus, dissociated vertical divergence, and sensorial suppression of the nonfixating eye, indicating that DHD develops only when binocular visual input is preempted early in life.3-6Some cases arise spontaneously, but most patients have undergone previous bimedial recessions.5 Originally attributed to unequal convergence damping of latent nystagmus,1,2it is now clear that this variable exodeviation is driven by a change in the sensory balance of visual inputs from both eyes.7In patients with DHD, monocular fixation induces a dissociated esodeviation (greater during fixation with the nonpreferred eye) that is usually superimposed on an exotropic resting position of the eyes (as found under nondepolarizing general anesthesia). Thus, when the baseline vergence position of the eyes is orthotropic, DHD can generate an esodeviation of variable amplitude in both eyes. Gräf et al8described this phenomenon in a patient who presented with unilateral accommodative esotropia. This patient’s eyes were aligned when examined under nondepolarizing anesthesia (Figure 2), confirming that DHD must arise from excessive esotonus during conditions of monocular fixation. The oscillopsia resulted from her latent nystagmus, which manifested during periods of intense fixation and esodeviation. The initial confirmatory test for DHD is the reversed fixation test (choice C).9After measuring the horizontal deviation in the nonfixating eye using alternate cover testing, the occluder is shifted back to the nonfixating eye, which normally shows no movement because the horizontal deviation has already been neutralized by the prism. In DHD, however, a horizontal movement of the fixating eye is seen, showing the presence of fixation-dependent innervation.9,10 The differential diagnosis of intermittent esotropia in adulthood includes decompensating esotropia (often caused by early presbyopia, necessitating excessive accommodative effort), anisometropia, and DHD. Retinoscopy ruled out anisometropia. An esodeviation produced by excessive accommodative effort owing to early presbyopia would be symmetrical in both eyes. Forced duction testing (choice A) was not indicated as ocular rotations were full. The absence of diplopia and the presence of latent nystagmus showed that this esotropia arose from a long-standing strabismus rather than a new-onset neurologic condition. Magnetic resonance imaging (choice B) was therefore not warranted. An increase in the exodeviation during periods of inattention (ie, nonfixation) is a useful clinical clue to the diagnosis of DHD.10In this patient, resolution of the esodeviation (due to suspension of dissociated esotonus) was seen during periods of nonfixation. Genetic testing (choice D) was not indicated as infantile strabismus is rarely hereditary, and she had no family history of strabismus. The patient was treated with small bilateral lateral rectus resections, which produced a consecutive exotropia. After small bilateral lateral rectus recessions, her eyes were straight at distance and near, and her symptoms abated.

caption: Clinical photographs of the left eye showing a diffuse yellow-pink lesion on the inferior palpebral conjunctiva (arrowheads) (A), and the yellow velvety appearance of the upper palpebral conjunctiva (arrowheads) (B).
scenario: A 73-year-old man was referred to our service for assessment of a slow-growing conjunctival lesion in the left eye. He had first noticed left eye discomfort and a fullness of the left lower eyelid 3 months previously. He denied any vision or systemic symptoms. His ophthalmic history was noncontributory. The patient’s medical history was notable only for prostate carcinoma, which was treated with radiotherapy 12 years ago. On examination, his visual acuities were 20/25 OU. Slitlamp examination of the anterior segment revealed diffuse yellow-pink polypoidal papules affecting the inferior fornix and inferior palpebral conjunctiva of the left eye (Figure 1A). The upper palpebral conjunctiva in the left eye had a velvety yellow appearance (Figure 1B). The remainder of the examination of both eyes was unremarkable. Initial investigations, including a complete blood cell count, urinalysis, and measurement of inflammatory markers, kidney function, and prostate-specific antigen level, were within normal limits. Serum electrophoresis showed raised monoclonal IgM bands (7.25 g/L; reference range, 0.50-2.00 g/L) with a κ/λ light-chain ratio of 2.92 (reference range, 0.260-1.65).

options.A: Commence lubricating eye drops and topical corticosteroids
options.B: Perform a complete excisional biopsy of the lesion
options.C: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits
options.D: Perform an incisional biopsy of the lesion

answer: Perform an incisional biopsy of the lesion
distractors: Commence lubricating eye drops and topical corticosteroids
Perform a complete excisional biopsy of the lesion
Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits
explanation: D. Perform an incisional biopsy of the lesion The appearance of this conjunctival lesion is suggestive of amyloidosis. Amyloid is an insoluble, fibrillar protein that can form tissue deposits, leading to functional impairment. The kidneys and heart are the most commonly affected organs in systemic amyloidosis. Primary localized conjunctival amyloidosis is a rare but well-described entity, most frequently affecting the palpebral conjunctiva and superior fornix.1The diagnosis of amyloidosis is based on its characteristic histologic features that help differentiate it from other conditions, such as malignant neoplasms (lymphoma, squamous, or sebaceous cell carcinomas) and inflammatory disorders (pyogenic granuloma, sarcoidosis). Clinically, it is most easily distinguished from a more defined, pedunculated, and highly vascular pyogenic granuloma. Amyloid characteristically stains with Congo red and exhibits apple-green birefringence on polarization microscopy examination (Figure 2). Therefore, an incisional biopsy should be performed (choice D) for diagnostic purposes. This can also provide symptomatic relief by debulking the conjunctival mass with an estimated recurrence rate of less than 30%.1A complete excisional biopsy (choice B) may be performed for solitary or more confined lesions, but it is less suitable for diffuse involvement of the conjunctiva as in this case.1,2Unlike inflammatory conditions, localized conjunctival amyloidosis does not respond to corticosteroid therapy (choice A). Lubricants can provide temporary symptomatic relief; however, surgical debulking remains the mainstay of therapy. If orbital amyloidosis causes substantial ptosis, proptosis, or eye movement restrictions, further surgical intervention and targeted external beam radiotherapy may be considered.3,4 Histologic examination confirmed conjunctival amyloidosis of no specific subtype in this patient. More than 20 different types of amyloid protein have been described. Secondary amyloidosis occurs in the context of systemic conditions, leading to the accumulation of AA amyloid derived from the acute-phase protein serum amyloid A. In primary amyloidosis, immunoglobulin light-chain–derived protein (AL) deposits in tissues. The condition may be localized or associated with an underlying plasma cell disorder. In a small proportion of patients, systemic AL amyloidosis may eventually progress to multiple myeloma,5whereas systemic AL amyloidosis may subsequently develop in approximately 1% of patients with multiple myeloma; this development confers a poor prognosis.6 Conjunctival amyloidosis is usually primary and localized, with no systemic associations.1,4However, a basic examination to rule out systemic disease is recommended.1Investigations typically include a complete blood cell count, bone profile, kidney and liver function tests, urinalysis, and serum and urine electrophoresis.1Presence of monoclonal gammopathy warrants further hematologic assessment by performing a bone marrow biopsy to exclude underlying multiple myeloma and other blood dyscrasias. Finally, ordering imaging of the orbits is useful to determine the extent of the condition, including any orbital involvement.2,4 Performing the incisional biopsy sufficiently debulked the lesion to alleviate the patient’s ocular symptoms. At the 6-month follow-up, the conjunctival appearance remained stable. Systemic examination findings, including magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits, bone marrow aspirate, and transthoracic echocardiogram, were unremarkable. Despite an elevated IgM level, no underlying plasma cell dyscrasia was identified. The patient continues to receive regular examinations from the oculoplastics service and has been referred to the National Amyloidosis Center.
